items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: What's in a name? That which we call a rose, By any other name would smell as sweet.
items.sourceLine: What's in a name? That which we call a rose, By any other name would smell as sweet.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Whose property is my body? Probably mine. I so regard it. If I experiment with it, who must be answerable? I, not the State. If I choose injudiciously, does the State die? Oh no.
items.sourceLine: Whose property is my body? Probably mine. I so regard it. If I experiment with it, who must be answerable? I, not the State. If I choose injudiciously, does the State die? Oh no.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: For what are they all in their high conceit, When man in the bush with God may meet?
items.sourceLine: For what are they all in their high conceit, When man in the bush with God may meet?

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: Here while I lie beneath this walnut bough, What care I for the Greeks or for Troy town, If juster battles are enacted now Between the ants upon this hummock's crown?
items.sourceLine: Here while I lie beneath this walnut bough, What care I for the Greeks or for Troy town, If juster battles are enacted now Between the ants upon this hummock's crown?

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The man of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in his speech. When a man feels the difficulty of doing, can he be other than cautious and slow in speaking?
items.sourceLine: The man of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in his speech. When a man feels the difficulty of doing, can he be other than cautious and slow in speaking?

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: Since before time and space were, the Tao is. It is beyond is and is not. How do I know this is true? I look inside myself and see.
items.sourceLine: Since before time and space were, the Tao is. It is beyond is and is not. How do I know this is true? I look inside myself and see.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: What dreadful hot weather we have! It keeps one in a continual state of inelegance.
items.sourceLine: What dreadful hot weather we have! It keeps one in a continual state of inelegance.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Now about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came out everyone has been enraptured by her? They say she is amazingly beautiful.
items.sourceLine: Now about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came out everyone has been enraptured by her? They say she is amazingly beautiful.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: When… in the course of all these thousands of years has man ever acted in accordance with his own interests?
items.sourceLine: When... in the course of all these thousands of years has man ever acted in accordance with his own interests?

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: I myself smoke, but my wife asked me to speak today on the harmfulness of tobacco, so what can I do? If it’s tobacco, then let it be tobacco.
items.sourceLine: I myself smoke, but my wife asked me to speak today on the harmfulness of tobacco, so what can I do? If it’s tobacco, then let it be tobacco.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Is a fixed income not a good thing? Does not everyone love to count on a sure thing? Especially every petty-bourgeois, narrow-minded Frenchman? the 'ever needy' man?
items.sourceLine: Is a fixed income not a good thing? Does not everyone love to count on a sure thing? Especially every petty-bourgeois, narrow-minded Frenchman? the 'ever needy' man?

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Was he an animal, that music could move him so? He felt as if the way to the unknown nourishment he longed for were coming to light.
items.sourceLine: Was he an animal, that music could move him so? He felt as if the way to the unknown nourishment he longed for were coming to light.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Is it reasonable to assume a purposiveness in all the parts of nature and to deny it to the whole?
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: Is it reasonable to assume a purposiveness in all the parts of nature and to deny it to the whole?

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: So gewiß ist der allein glücklich und groß, der weder zu herrschen noch zu gehorchen braucht, um etwas zu sein!
items.sourceLine: So gewiß ist der allein glücklich und groß, der weder zu herrschen noch zu gehorchen braucht, um etwas zu sein!

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Is Wagner a human being at all? Is he not rather a disease? He contaminates everything he touches - he has made music sick.
items.sourceLine: Is Wagner a human being at all? Is he not rather a disease? He contaminates everything he touches - he has made music sick.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Rascals are always sociable — more’s the pity! and the chief sign that a man has any nobility in his character is the little pleasure he takes in others’ company.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: Rascals are always sociable — more’s the pity! and the chief sign that a man has any nobility in his character is the little pleasure he takes in others’ company.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: Is Christ only to be adored? Or is the holy Mother of God rather not to be honoured? This is the woman who crushed the Serpent's head. Hear us. For your Son denies you nothing.
items.sourceLine: Is Christ only to be adored? Or is the holy Mother of God rather not to be honoured? This is the woman who crushed the Serpent's head. Hear us. For your Son denies you nothing.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Me tenant comme je suis, un pied dans un pays et l'autre en un autre, je trouve ma condition très heureuse, en ce qu'elle est libre.
items.sourceLine: Me tenant comme je suis, un pied dans un pays et l'autre en un autre, je trouve ma condition très heureuse, en ce qu'elle est libre.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: What then remains but that we still should cry Not to be born, or, being born, to die?
items.sourceLine: What then remains but that we still should cry Not to be born, or, being born, to die?

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: How I know that my philosophy is the best among all that have ever been taught in the world, or are being taught, or ever will be taught?
items.sourceLine: You seem to wish to employ reason, and ask me, "How I know that my philosophy is the best among all that have ever been taught in the world, or are being taught, or ever will be taught?" a question which I might with much greater right ask you ; for I do not presume that I have found the best philosophy, I know that I understand the true philosophy. If you ask in what way I know it, I answer: In the same way as you k

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: To love is to be delighted by the happiness of someone, or to experience pleasure upon the happiness of another. I define this as true love.
items.sourceLine: To love is to be delighted by the happiness of someone, or to experience pleasure upon the happiness of another. I define this as true love.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: What would become of history, had we not a dependence on the veracity of the historian, according to the experience, what we have had of mankind?
items.sourceLine: What would become of history, had we not a dependence on the veracity of the historian, according to the experience, what we have had of mankind?

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The Union was a measure from which infinite Good has been derived to this country.
items.sourceLine: The Union was a measure from which infinite Good has been derived to this country.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: How can great minds be produced in a country where the test of a great mind is agreeing in the opinions of small minds?
items.sourceLine: How can great minds be produced in a country where the test of a great mind is agreeing in the opinions of small minds?

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: At first I was almost about to despair, I thought I never could bear it — but I did bear it. The question remains: how?
items.sourceLine: At first I was almost about to despair, I thought I never could bear it — but I did bear it. The question remains: how?

items.author: Giosuè Carducci
items.quote: Il sole / ridea calando dietro il Resegone
items.sourceLine: Il sole / ridea calando dietro il Resegone

items.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
items.quote: Der Mensch, wo ist er her? Zu schlecht für einen Gott, zu gut fürs Ungefähr.
items.sourceLine: Der Mensch, wo ist er her? Zu schlecht für einen Gott, zu gut fürs Ungefähr.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Was it not the most wonderful thing on earth to be able to help one's fellow-creatures? I now knew that it was the only thing that was worth while.
items.sourceLine: Was it not the most wonderful thing on earth to be able to help one's fellow-creatures? I now knew that it was the only thing that was worth while.

items.author: Dante Alighieri
items.quote: In quella parte del libro de la mia memoria, dinanzi a la quale poco si potrebbe leggere, si trova una rubrica, la quale dice: Incipit vita nova.
items.sourceLine: In quella parte del libro de la mia memoria, dinanzi a la quale poco si potrebbe leggere, si trova una rubrica, la quale dice: Incipit vita nova.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: And, after all, what is a fashion? From the artistic point of view, it is usually a form of ugliness so intolerable that we have to alter it every six months.
items.sourceLine: And, after all, what is a fashion? From the artistic point of view, it is usually a form of ugliness so intolerable that we have to alter it every six months.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Happy, even in anguish, is he to whom God has given a soul worthy of love and of grief!
items.sourceLine: Happy, even in anguish, is he to whom God has given a soul worthy of love and of grief!

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: What is asked of a man that he may be able to pray for his enemies? To pray for one's enemies is the hardest thing of all. That is why it exasperates us so much in our present day situation.
items.sourceLine: What is asked of a man that he may be able to pray for his enemies? To pray for one's enemies is the hardest thing of all. That is why it exasperates us so much in our present day situation.

items.author: Catherine II of Russia
items.quote: A great wind is blowing, and that gives you either imagination or a headache.
items.sourceLine: A great wind is blowing, and that gives you either imagination or a headache.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: I am Richard II know ye not that? … He that will forget God, will also forget his benefactors; this tragedy was played 40 times in open streets and houses.
items.sourceLine: I am Richard II know ye not that? ... He that will forget God, will also forget his benefactors; this tragedy was played 40 times in open streets and houses.

items.author: Victoria of the United Kingdom
items.quote: Affairs go on, and all will take some shape or other, but it keeps one in hot water all the time.
items.sourceLine: Affairs go on, and all will take some shape or other, but it keeps one in hot water all the time.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: For what is life but a play in which everyone acts a part until the curtain comes down?
items.sourceLine: For what is life but a play in which everyone acts a part until the curtain comes down?

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Combien de choses nous servoyent hier d’articles de foy, qui nous sont fables aujourd’huy?
items.sourceLine: Combien de choses nous servoyent hier d’articles de foy, qui nous sont fables aujourd’huy?

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: The Living Bread from Heaven With figures doth away: O wondrous gift indeed! The poor and lowly may Upon their Lord and Master feed.
items.sourceLine: Thus Angels' Bread is made The Bread of man today: The Living Bread from Heaven With figures doth away: O wondrous gift indeed! The poor and lowly may Upon their Lord and Master feed.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Augustine, Augustine, quid quaeris? Putasne brevi immettere vasculo mare totum?
items.sourceLine: Augustine, Augustine, quid quaeris? Putasne brevi immettere vasculo mare totum?

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Catch then, O! catch the transient hour, Improve each moment as it flies; Life's a short Summer — man a flower, He dies — alas! how soon he dies!
items.sourceLine: Catch then, O! catch the transient hour, Improve each moment as it flies; Life's a short Summer — man a flower, He dies — alas! how soon he dies!

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: Rien n'est humiliant comme de voir les sots réussir dans les entreprises où l'on échoue.
items.sourceLine: Rien n'est humiliant comme de voir les sots réussir dans les entreprises où l'on échoue.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Lorsque les femmes nous aiment, elles nous pardonnent tout, même nos crimes; lorsqu'elles ne nous aiment pas, elles ne nous pardonnent rien, pas même nos vertus!
items.sourceLine: Lorsque les femmes nous aiment, elles nous pardonnent tout, même nos crimes ; lorsqu'elles ne nous aiment pas, elles ne nous pardonnent rien, pas même nos vertus !

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Je fais toujours bien le premier vers: mais j'ai peine à faire les autres.
items.sourceLine: Je fais toujours bien le premier vers: mais j'ai peine à faire les autres.

items.author: Franz Rosenzweig
items.quote: Philosophy takes it upon itself to throw off the fear of things earthly, to rob death of its poisonous sting.
items.sourceLine: Philosophy takes it upon itself to throw off the fear of things earthly, to rob death of its poisonous sting.

items.author: Leopold Kronecker
items.quote: Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk.
items.sourceLine: Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk.

items.author: Rudolf Otto
items.quote: These materials are found in India, in more primitive forms not merely as a late period but in the remotest pre-Christian Kausitakt Upanishad.
items.sourceLine: These materials are found in India, in more primitive forms not merely as a late period but in the remotest pre-Christian Kausitakt Upanishad.

items.author: Alexander von Humboldt
items.quote: Only what we have wrought into our character during life can we take away with us.
items.sourceLine: Only what we have wrought into our character during life can we take away with us.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, That ever I was born to set it right!
items.sourceLine: The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, That ever I was born to set it right!

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Enough, enough, enough! Say no more! Lump the whole thing! say that the Creator made Italy from designs by Michael Angelo!
items.sourceLine: Enough, enough, enough! Say no more! Lump the whole thing! say that the Creator made Italy from designs by Michael Angelo!

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: It costs a beautiful person no exertion to paint her image on our eyes; yet how splendid is that benefit! It costs no more for a wise soul to convey his quality to other men.
items.sourceLine: It costs a beautiful person no exertion to paint her image on our eyes; yet how splendid is that benefit! It costs no more for a wise soul to convey his quality to other men.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: When will the world learn that a million men are of no importance compared with one man?
items.sourceLine: When will the world learn that a million men are of no importance compared with one man?

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The superior man has neither anxiety nor fear. When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?
items.sourceLine: The superior man has neither anxiety nor fear. When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: The Tao is like a bellows: it is empty yet infinitely capable. The more you use it, the more it produces; the more you talk of it, the less you understand.
items.sourceLine: The Tao is like a bellows: it is empty yet infinitely capable. The more you use it, the more it produces; the more you talk of it, the less you understand.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbors and laugh at them in our turn?
items.sourceLine: For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbors and laugh at them in our turn?

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly. It is the one thing we are interested in here.
items.sourceLine: Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly. It is the one thing we are interested in here.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: And now once again I asked myself the question: do I love her? And once more I could not answer, that is to say, again, for the hundredth time, I answered that I hated her.
items.sourceLine: And now once again I asked myself the question: do I love her? And once more I could not answer, that is to say, again, for the hundredth time, I answered that I hated her.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: You look at any poetic creature: muslin, ether, demigoddess, millions of delights; then you look into the soul and find the most ordinary crocodile!
items.sourceLine: You look at any poetic creature: muslin, ether, demigoddess, millions of delights; then you look into the soul and find the most ordinary crocodile!

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Lincoln's place in the history of the United States and of mankind will, nevertheless, be next to that of Washington!
items.section: Comments on the North American Events (1862)
items.sourceLine: Lincoln's place in the history of the United States and of mankind will, nevertheless, be next to that of Washington!

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Like a dog!" he said, it was as if the shame of it should outlive him.
items.sourceLine: "Like a dog!" he said, it was as if the shame of it should outlive him.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: All the interests of my reason, speculative as well as practical, combine in the three following questions: 1. What can I know? 2. What ought I to do? 3. What may I hope?
items.sourceLine: All the interests of my reason, speculative as well as practical, combine in the three following questions: 1. What can I know? 2. What ought I to do? 3. What may I hope?

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Noble be man, Helpful and good! For that alone Sets hims apart From every other creature On earth.
items.sourceLine: Noble be man, Helpful and good! For that alone Sets hims apart From every other creature On earth.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Be clever, Ariadne! … You have little ears; you have my ears: Put a clever word in them! — Must one not first hate oneself, in order to love oneself? … I am your labyrinth …
items.sourceLine: Dionysus: Be clever, Ariadne! ... You have little ears; you have my ears: Put a clever word in them! — Must one not first hate oneself, in order to love oneself? ... I am your labyrinth ...

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Because people have no thoughts to deal in, they deal cards, and try and win one another’s money. Idiots!
items.section: Not yet placed by volume, chapter or section
items.sourceLine: Because people have no thoughts to deal in, they deal cards, and try and win one another’s money. Idiots!

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: By God's grace, I know Satan very well. If Satan can turn God's Word upside down and pervert the Scriptures, what will he do with my words -- or the words of others?
items.sourceLine: By God's grace, I know Satan very well. If Satan can turn God's Word upside down and pervert the Scriptures, what will he do with my words -- or the words of others?

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: The entire method consists in the order and arrangement of the things to which the mind's eye must turn so that we can discover some truth.
items.sourceLine: The entire method consists in the order and arrangement of the things to which the mind's eye must turn so that we can discover some truth.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Libraries are as the shrine where all the relics of the ancient saints, full of true virtue, and that without delusion or imposture, are preserved and reposed.
items.sourceLine: Libraries are as the shrine where all the relics of the ancient saints, full of true virtue, and that without delusion or imposture, are preserved and reposed.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Do you remember Goethe's wise words about reading Spinoza? — “I always preferred knowing what an author himself said, to knowing what others thought he ought to have said.
items.sourceLine: Do you remember Goethe's wise words about reading Spinoza? — “I always preferred knowing what an author himself said, to knowing what others thought he ought to have said.”

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: Chaque substance est comme un monde à part, indépendant de toute autre chose, hors de Dieu…
items.sourceLine: Chaque substance est comme un monde à part, indépendant de toute autre chose, hors de Dieu...

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: The life of man is of no greater importance to the universe than that of an oyster.
items.sourceLine: The life of man is of no greater importance to the universe than that of an oyster.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Hatred and anger are the greatest poison to the happiness of a good mind.
items.sourceLine: Hatred and anger are the greatest poison to the happiness of a good mind.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: It is not because men's desires are strong that they act ill; it is because their consciences are weak.
items.sourceLine: It is not because men's desires are strong that they act ill; it is because their consciences are weak.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: So we keep asking, over and over, Until a handful of earth Stops our mouths — But is that an answer?
items.sourceLine: So we keep asking, over and over, Until a handful of earth Stops our mouths — But is that an answer?

items.author: Giosuè Carducci
items.quote: To thee of All Being /A te, de l’essere
items.sourceLine: To thee of All Being /A te, de l’essere

items.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
items.quote: Denn zu einem großen Manne gehört beides: Kleinigkeiten als Kleinigkeiten, und wichtige Dinge als wichtige Dinge zu behandeln.
items.sourceLine: Denn zu einem großen Manne gehört beides: Kleinigkeiten als Kleinigkeiten, und wichtige Dinge als wichtige Dinge zu behandeln.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Immanuel Kant lived with knowledge as with his lawfully wedded wife, slept with it in the same intellectual bed for forty years and begot an entire German race of philosophical systems.
items.sourceLine: Immanuel Kant lived with knowledge as with his lawfully wedded wife, slept with it in the same intellectual bed for forty years and begot an entire German race of philosophical systems.

items.author: Dante Alighieri
items.quote: Ella è quanto de ben pò far natura; per essemplo di lei bieltà si prova.
items.sourceLine: Ella è quanto de ben pò far natura; per essemplo di lei bieltà si prova.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Lo! with a little rod I did but touch the honey of romance — And must I lose a soul's inheritance?
items.sourceLine: Lo! with a little rod I did but touch the honey of romance — And must I lose a soul's inheritance?

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: To love or to have loved, that is enough. Ask nothing further. There is no other pearl to be found in the dark folds of life. To love is a consummation.
items.sourceLine: To love or to have loved, that is enough. Ask nothing further. There is no other pearl to be found in the dark folds of life. To love is a consummation.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: How absurd men are! They never use the liberties they have, they demand those they do not have. They have freedom of thought, they demand freedom of speech.
items.sourceLine: How absurd men are! They never use the liberties they have, they demand those they do not have. They have freedom of thought, they demand freedom of speech.

items.author: Catherine II of Russia
items.quote: You philosophers are lucky men. You write on paper and paper is patient. Unfortunate Empress that I am, I write on the susceptible skins of living beings.
items.sourceLine: You philosophers are lucky men. You write on paper and paper is patient. Unfortunate Empress that I am, I write on the susceptible skins of living beings.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Must is not a word to be used to princes! Little man, little man, if your father had lived, ye durst not have said so much: but thou knowest I must die, and that maketh thee so presumptuous.
items.sourceLine: Must is not a word to be used to princes! Little man, little man, if your father had lived, ye durst not have said so much: but thou knowest I must die, and that maketh thee so presumptuous.

items.author: Victoria of the United Kingdom
items.quote: We are not interested in the possibilities of defeat; they do not exist.
items.sourceLine: We are not interested in the possibilities of defeat; they do not exist.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Of how much more passion than reason has Jupiter composed us? putting in, as one would say, "scarce half an ounce to a pound.
items.sourceLine: Of how much more passion than reason has Jupiter composed us? putting in, as one would say, "scarce half an ounce to a pound."

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Quelle vérité que ces montagnes bornent, qui est mensonge qui se tient au delà?
items.sourceLine: Quelle vérité que ces montagnes bornent, qui est mensonge qui se tient au delà?

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Thus Angels' Bread is made The Bread of man today: The Living Bread from Heaven With figures doth away: O wondrous gift indeed! The poor and lowly may Upon their Lord and Master feed.
items.sourceLine: Thus Angels' Bread is made The Bread of man today: The Living Bread from Heaven With figures doth away: O wondrous gift indeed! The poor and lowly may Upon their Lord and Master feed.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova, sero te amavi! et ecce intus eras et ego foris, et ibi te quaerebam.
items.sourceLine: Sero te amavi, pulchritudo tam antiqua et tam nova, sero te amavi! et ecce intus eras et ego foris, et ibi te quaerebam.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Ah! let not Censure term our fate our choice, The stage but echoes back the public's voice; The drama's laws the drama's patrons give, For we that live to please must please to live.
items.section: Prologue at the Opening of Drury Lane Theatre (1747)
items.sourceLine: Ah! let not Censure term our fate our choice, The stage but echoes back the public's voice; The drama's laws the drama's patrons give, For we that live to please must please to live.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: He is so corrupt that he would willingly pay for the pleasure of selling himself.
items.sourceLine: He is so corrupt that he would willingly pay for the pleasure of selling himself.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: La vie n'est-elle pas une machine à laquelle l'argent imprime le mouvement?
items.sourceLine: La vie n'est-elle pas une machine à laquelle l'argent imprime le mouvement ?

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Presque tous les hommes meurent de leurs remèdes, et non pas de leurs maladies.
items.sourceLine: Presque tous les hommes meurent de leurs remèdes, et non pas de leurs maladies.

items.author: Alexander von Humboldt
items.quote: The expression of vanity and self-love becomes less offensive, when it retains something of simplicity and frankness.
items.sourceLine: The expression of vanity and self-love becomes less offensive, when it retains something of simplicity and frankness.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: What a piece of work is a man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! In form and moving how express and admirable! In action how like an angel, in apprehension how like a god!
items.sourceLine: What a piece of work is a man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! In form and moving how express and admirable! In action how like an angel, in apprehension how like a god!

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: H'aint we got all the fools in town on our side? And ain't that a big enough majority in any town?
items.sourceLine: H'aint we got all the fools in town on our side? And ain't that a big enough majority in any town?

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Is not marriage an open question, when it is alleged, from the beginning of the world, that such as are in the institution wish to get out, and such as are out wish to get in?
items.sourceLine: Is not marriage an open question, when it is alleged, from the beginning of the world, that such as are in the institution wish to get out, and such as are out wish to get in?

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
items.sourceLine: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Perfect is the virtue which is according to the Mean! Rare have they long been among the people, who could practice it!
items.sourceLine: Perfect is the virtue which is according to the Mean! Rare have they long been among the people, who could practice it!

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: The Tao is called the Great Mother: empty yet inexhaustible, it gives birth to infinite worlds.
items.sourceLine: The Tao is called the Great Mother: empty yet inexhaustible, it gives birth to infinite worlds.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: …why did we wait for any thing? — why not seize the pleasure at once? — How often is happiness destroyed by preparation, foolish preparation!
items.sourceLine: ...why did we wait for any thing? — why not seize the pleasure at once? — How often is happiness destroyed by preparation, foolish preparation!

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Can it be that I have overlooked something, that there is something which I have failed to understand? Is it not possible that this state of despair is common to everyone?
items.sourceLine: Several times I asked myself, "Can it be that I have overlooked something, that there is something which I have failed to understand? Is it not possible that this state of despair is common to everyone?" And I searched for an answer to my questions in every area of knowledge acquired by man. For a long time I carried on my painstaking search; I did not search casually, out of mere curiosity, but painfully, persistent

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Is it really not possible to touch the gaming table without being instantly infected by superstition?
items.sourceLine: Is it really not possible to touch the gaming table without being instantly infected by superstition?

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: How pleasant it is to respect people! When I see books, I am not concerned with how the authors loved or played cards; I see only their marvelous works.
items.sourceLine: How pleasant it is to respect people! When I see books, I am not concerned with how the authors loved or played cards; I see only their marvelous works.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Thus heaven I’ve forfeited, I know it full well. My soul, once true to God, is chosen for hell.
items.sourceLine: Thus heaven I’ve forfeited, I know it full well. My soul, once true to God, is chosen for hell.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Don't you want to join us?" I was recently asked by an acquaintance when he ran across me alone after midnight in a coffeehouse that was already almost deserted. "No, I don't," I said.
items.sourceLine: "Don't you want to join us?" I was recently asked by an acquaintance when he ran across me alone after midnight in a coffeehouse that was already almost deserted. "No, I don't," I said.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: The wish to talk to God is absurd. We cannot talk to one we cannot comprehend — and we cannot comprehend God; we can only believe in Him. The uses of prayer are thus only subjective.
items.sourceLine: The wish to talk to God is absurd. We cannot talk to one we cannot comprehend — and we cannot comprehend God; we can only believe in Him. The uses of prayer are thus only subjective.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Willst du immer weiterschweifen? Sieh, das Gute liegt so nah. Lerne nur das Glück ergreifen, denn das Glück ist immer da.
items.sourceLine: Willst du immer weiterschweifen? Sieh, das Gute liegt so nah. Lerne nur das Glück ergreifen, denn das Glück ist immer da.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Dionysus: Be clever, Ariadne! … You have little ears; you have my ears: Put a clever word in them!
items.sourceLine: Dionysus: Be clever, Ariadne! ... You have little ears; you have my ears: Put a clever word in them! — Must one not first hate oneself, in order to love oneself? ... I am your labyrinth ...

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: We forfeit three-fourths of ourselves in order to be like other people.
items.sourceLine: We forfeit three-fourths of ourselves in order to be like other people.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: If a woman becomes weary and at last dead from bearing, that matters not; let her only die from bearing, she is there to do it.
items.sourceLine: If a woman becomes weary and at last dead from bearing, that matters not; let her only die from bearing, she is there to do it.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: In order to seek truth, it is necessary once in the course of our life, to doubt, as far as possible, of all things.
items.sourceLine: In order to seek truth, it is necessary once in the course of our life, to doubt, as far as possible, of all things.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Nay, number (itself) in armies, importeth not much, where the people is of weak courage; for (as Virgil saith) it never troubles the wolf how many the sheep be.
items.sourceLine: Nay, number (itself) in armies, importeth not much, where the people is of weak courage; for (as Virgil saith) it never troubles the wolf how many the sheep be.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: If Goethe would only for once pick up some other Latin book than Spinoza!
items.sourceLine: To express myself briefly, Goethe was the Spinoza of poetry. The whole of Goethe's poetry is filled with the same spirit that is wafted toward us from the writings of Spinoza. There is no doubt whatsoever that Goethe paid undivided allegiance to Spinoza's doctrine. items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: Musica est exercitium arithmeticae occultum nescientis se numerare animi.
items.sourceLine: Musica est exercitium arithmeticae occultum nescientis se numerare animi.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Nature may certainly produce whatever can arise from habit: Nay, habit is nothing but one of the principles of nature, and derives all its force from that origin.
items.sourceLine: Nature may certainly produce whatever can arise from habit: Nay, habit is nothing but one of the principles of nature, and derives all its force from that origin.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: We are delighted to find a person who values us as we value ourselves, and distinguishes us from the rest of mankind, with an attention not unlike that with which we distinguish ourselves.
items.sourceLine: We are delighted to find a person who values us as we value ourselves, and distinguishes us from the rest of mankind, with an attention not unlike that with which we distinguish ourselves.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being.
items.sourceLine: I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Oh what lies there are in kisses! And their guile so well prepared! Sweet the snaring is; but this is Sweeter still, to be ensnared.
items.sourceLine: Oh what lies there are in kisses! And their guile so well prepared! Sweet the snaring is; but this is Sweeter still, to be ensnared.

items.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
items.quote: Kleinigkeiten als Kleinigkeiten, und wichtige Dinge als wichtige Dinge zu behandeln.
items.sourceLine: Denn zu einem großen Manne gehört beides: Kleinigkeiten als Kleinigkeiten, und wichtige Dinge als wichtige Dinge zu behandeln.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Supreme achievement and outstanding capacity are only rendered possible by mental concentration, by a sublime monomania that verges on lunacy.
items.sourceLine: Supreme achievement and outstanding capacity are only rendered possible by mental concentration, by a sublime monomania that verges on lunacy.

items.author: Dante Alighieri
items.quote: Amore e 'l cor gentil sono una cosa… e così esser l'un sanza l'altro osa com'alma razional sanza ragione.
items.sourceLine: Amore e 'l cor gentil sono una cosa... e così esser l'un sanza l'altro osa com'alma razional sanza ragione.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Why, what a wonderful piece of luck! Here is a red rose! I have never seen any rose like it in all my life. It is so beautiful that I am sure it has a long Latin name.
items.section: The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)
items.sourceLine: Why, what a wonderful piece of luck! Here is a red rose! I have never seen any rose like it in all my life. It is so beautiful that I am sure it has a long Latin name.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Il y a maintenant en France dans chaque village un flambeau allumé, le maître d'école, et une bouche qui souffle dessus, le curé.
items.sourceLine: Il y a maintenant en France dans chaque village un flambeau allumé, le maître d'école, et une bouche qui souffle dessus, le curé.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: There are many people who reach their conclusions about life like schoolboys; they cheat their master by copying the answer out of a book without having worked out the sum for themselves.
items.sourceLine: There are many people who reach their conclusions about life like schoolboys; they cheat their master by copying the answer out of a book without having worked out the sum for themselves.

items.author: Catherine II of Russia
items.quote: It is better to be subject to the Laws under one Master, than to be subservient to many.
items.section: Proposals for a New Law Code (1768)
items.sourceLine: It is better to be subject to the Laws under one Master, than to be subservient to many.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Twas God the Word that spake it, He took the Bread and brake it: And what that Word did make it, That I believe and take it.
items.sourceLine: 'Twas God the Word that spake it, He took the Bread and brake it: And what that Word did make it, That I believe and take it.

items.author: Victoria of the United Kingdom
items.quote: I am too horrified for words at this monstrous horrible sentence against this poor martyr Dreyfus. If only all Europe would express its horror and indignation! I trust there will be a severe retribution.
items.sourceLine: I am too horrified for words at this monstrous horrible sentence against this poor martyr Dreyfus. If only all Europe would express its horror and indignation! I trust there will be a severe retribution.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: You must acquire the best knowledge first, and without delay; it is the height of madness to learn what you will later have to unlearn.
items.sourceLine: You must acquire the best knowledge first, and without delay; it is the height of madness to learn what you will later have to unlearn.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: When I play with my cat, who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me?
items.sourceLine: When I play with my cat, who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me?

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Bene scripsísti de me, Thoma; quam ergo mercédem accípies? Aquinas: Non áliam, Dómine, nisi teípsum.
items.sourceLine: Jesus Christ: Bene scripsísti de me, Thoma; quam ergo mercédem accípies? Aquinas: Non áliam, Dómine, nisi teípsum.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio.
items.sourceLine: Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Enlarge my life with multitude of days!" In health, in sickness, thus the suppliant prays: Hides from himself his state, and shuns to know That life protracted is protracted woe.
items.sourceLine: "Enlarge my life with multitude of days!" In health, in sickness, thus the suppliant prays: Hides from himself his state, and shuns to know That life protracted is protracted woe.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: One must not always think that feeling is everything. Art is nothing without form.
items.sourceLine: One must not always think that feeling is everything. Art is nothing without form.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Je réussirai!" Le mot du joueur, du grand capitaine, mot fataliste qui perd plus d'hommes qu'il n'en sauve.
items.sourceLine: "Je réussirai !" Le mot du joueur, du grand capitaine, mot fataliste qui perd plus d'hommes qu'il n'en sauve.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Ceux de qui la conduite offre le plus à rire Sont toujours sur autrui les premiers à médire.
items.sourceLine: Ceux de qui la conduite offre le plus à rire Sont toujours sur autrui les premiers à médire.

items.author: Alexander von Humboldt
items.quote: Our imagination is struck only by what is great; but the lover of natural philosophy should reflect equally on little things.
items.sourceLine: Our imagination is struck only by what is great; but the lover of natural philosophy should reflect equally on little things.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: With this same key Shakespeare unlocked his heart," once more! Did Shakespeare? If so, the less Shakespeare he!
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: "With this same key Shakespeare unlocked his heart," once more! Did Shakespeare? If so, the less Shakespeare he!

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: What is the difference between a taxidermist & a tax-collector? The taxidermist only takes your skin.
items.sourceLine: What is the difference between a taxidermist & a tax-collector? The taxidermist only takes your skin.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Solvency is maintained by means of the national debt, on the principle, "If you will not lend me the money, how can I pay you?
items.sourceLine: Solvency is maintained by means of the national debt, on the principle, "If you will not lend me the money, how can I pay you?"

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: Unjust laws exist: shall we be content to obey them, or shall we endeavor to amend them, and obey them until we have succeeded, or shall we transgress them at once?
items.sourceLine: Unjust laws exist: shall we be content to obey them, or shall we endeavor to amend them, and obey them until we have succeeded, or shall we transgress them at once?

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: It is more shameful to distrust our friends than to be deceived by them.
items.sourceLine: It is more shameful to distrust our friends than to be deceived by them.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: By letting it go it all gets done. The world is won by those who let it go. But when you try and try, the world is beyond the winning.
items.sourceLine: By letting it go it all gets done. The world is won by those who let it go. But when you try and try, the world is beyond the winning.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: Here I am once more in this scene of dissipation and vice, and I begin already to find my morals corrupted.
items.sourceLine: Here I am once more in this scene of dissipation and vice, and I begin already to find my morals corrupted.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: One can only live while one is intoxicated with life; as soon as one is sober it is impossible not to see that it is all a mere fraud and a stupid fraud!
items.sourceLine: One can only live while one is intoxicated with life; as soon as one is sober it is impossible not to see that it is all a mere fraud and a stupid fraud!

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: … князь утверждает, что мир спасет красота! А я утверждаю, что у него оттого такие игривые мысли, что он теперь влюблен.
items.sourceLine: ... князь утверждает, что мир спасет красота! А я утверждаю, что у него оттого такие игривые мысли, что он теперь влюблен.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: The world is a fine place. The only thing wrong with it is us. How little justice and humility there is in us, how poorly we understand patriotism!
items.sourceLine: The world is a fine place. The only thing wrong with it is us. How little justice and humility there is in us, how poorly we understand patriotism!

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles.
items.sourceLine: The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: You asking me the way?" "Yes," I said, "since I can't find it myself." "Give it up! Give it up!" said he, and turned with a sudden jerk, like someone who wants to be alone with his laughter.
items.sourceLine: "You asking me the way?" "Yes," I said, "since I can't find it myself." "Give it up! Give it up!" said he, and turned with a sudden jerk, like someone who wants to be alone with his laughter.

items.quote: Religion is too important a matter to its devotees to be a subject of ridicule. If they indulge in absurdities, they are to be pitied rather than ridiculed.
items.sourceLine: Religion is too important a matter to its devotees to be a subject of ridicule. If they indulge in absurdities, they are to be pitied rather than ridiculed.

items.sourceLine: Knowledge, that tendeth but to satisfaction, is but as a courtesan, which is for pleasure, and not for fruit or generation.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The virtue of frugality lies in a middle between avarice and profusion, of which the one consists in an excess, the other in a defect of the proper attention to the objects of self–interest.
items.sourceLine: The virtue of frugality lies in a middle between avarice and profusion, of which the one consists in an excess, the other in a defect of the proper attention to the objects of self–interest.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Whatever crushes individuality is despotism, by whatever name it may be called, and whether it professes to be enforcing the will of God or the injunctions of men.
items.sourceLine: Whatever crushes individuality is despotism, by whatever name it may be called, and whether it professes to be enforcing the will of God or the injunctions of men.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: What! Think you that my flashes show me Only in lightnings to excel? Believe me, friends, you do not know me, For I can thunder quite as well.
items.sourceLine: What! Think you that my flashes show me Only in lightnings to excel? Believe me, friends, you do not know me, For I can thunder quite as well.

items.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
items.quote: I, who ne'er Went for myself a begging, go a borrowing, And that for others. Borrowing's much the same As begging; just as lending upon usury Is much the same as thieving.
items.sourceLine: I, who ne'er Went for myself a begging, go a borrowing, And that for others. Borrowing's much the same As begging; just as lending upon usury Is much the same as thieving.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: It is never until one realizes that one means something to others that one feels there is any point or purpose in one's own existence.
items.sourceLine: It is never until one realizes that one means something to others that one feels there is any point or purpose in one's own existence.

items.author: Dante Alighieri
items.quote: Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona de la mia donna disiosamente… che lo 'ntelletto sovr'esse disvia.
items.sourceLine: Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona de la mia donna disiosamente... che lo 'ntelletto sovr'esse disvia.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Ah! Don't say you agree with me. When people agree with me I always feel I must be wrong.
items.sourceLine: Ah! Don't say you agree with me. When people agree with me I always feel I must be wrong.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: On résiste à l'invasion des armées; on ne résiste pas à l'invasion des idées.
items.sourceLine: On résiste à l'invasion des armées; on ne résiste pas à l'invasion des idées.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: God creates out of nothing. Wonderful you say. Yes, to be sure, but He does what is still more wonderful: He makes saints out of sinners.
items.sourceLine: God creates out of nothing. Wonderful you say. Yes, to be sure, but He does what is still more wonderful: He makes saints out of sinners.

items.author: Catherine II of Russia
items.quote: The Laws ought to be so framed, as to secure the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible.
items.section: Proposals for a New Law Code (1768)
items.sourceLine: The Laws ought to be so framed, as to secure the Safety of every Citizen as much as possible.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Much suspected by me, Nothing proved can be, Quoth Elizabeth prisoner.
items.sourceLine: Much suspected by me, Nothing proved can be, Quoth Elizabeth prisoner.

items.author: Victoria of the United Kingdom
items.quote: It is worth being shot at to see how much one is loved.
items.sourceLine: It is worth being shot at to see how much one is loved.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Do not be guilty of possessing a library of learned books while lacking learning yourself.
items.sourceLine: Do not be guilty of possessing a library of learned books while lacking learning yourself.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: O God! thou mayest save me if thou wilt, and if thou wilt thou mayest destroy me; but whether or no, I will steer my rudder true.
items.sourceLine: The mariner of old said to Neptune in a great tempest, "O God! thou mayest save me if thou wilt, and if thou wilt thou mayest destroy me; but whether or no, I will steer my rudder true."

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Jesus Christ: Bene scripsísti de me, Thoma; quam ergo mercédem accípies? Aquinas: Non áliam, Dómine, nisi teípsum.
items.sourceLine: Jesus Christ: Bene scripsísti de me, Thoma; quam ergo mercédem accípies? Aquinas: Non áliam, Dómine, nisi teípsum.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: What is love's perfection? To love our enemies, and to love them to the end that they may be our brothers.
items.section: Ten Homilies on the First Epistle of John (414)
items.sourceLine: What is love's perfection? To love our enemies, and to love them to the end that they may be our brothers.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Fears of the brave, and follies of the wise! From Marlb'rough's eyes the streams of dotage flow, And Swift expires, a driv'ler and a show.
items.sourceLine: Fears of the brave, and follies of the wise! From Marlb'rough's eyes the streams of dotage flow, And Swift expires, a driv'ler and a show.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: To be stupid, selfish, and have good health are three requirements for happiness, though if stupidity is lacking, all is lost.
items.sourceLine: To be stupid, selfish, and have good health are three requirements for happiness, though if stupidity is lacking, all is lost.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: — Je suis tourmenté par de mauvaises idées. — En quel genre? Ça se guérit, les idées. - Comment? - En y succombant.
items.sourceLine: — Je suis tourmenté par de mauvaises idées. — En quel genre ? Ça se guérit, les idées. - Comment ? - En y succombant.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Couvrez ce sein que je ne saurais voir. Par de pareils objets les âmes sont blessées.
items.sourceLine: Couvrez ce sein que je ne saurais voir. Par de pareils objets les âmes sont blessées.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Voltaire and Shakespeare! He was all The other feigned to be. The flippant Frenchman speaks: I weep; And Shakespeare weeps with me.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: Voltaire and Shakespeare! He was all The other feigned to be. The flippant Frenchman speaks: I weep; And Shakespeare weeps with me.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: I haven't a particle of confidence in a man who has no redeeming petty vices whatsoever.
items.sourceLine: I haven't a particle of confidence in a man who has no redeeming petty vices whatsoever.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: To-day unbind the captive, So only are ye unbound; Lift up a people from the dust, Trump of their rescue, sound!
items.sourceLine: To-day unbind the captive, So only are ye unbound; Lift up a people from the dust, Trump of their rescue, sound!

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: There are various, nay, incredible faiths; why should we be alarmed at any of them? What man believes, God believes.
items.sourceLine: There are various, nay, incredible faiths; why should we be alarmed at any of them? What man believes, God believes.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The more man meditates upon good thoughts, the better will be his world and the world at large.
items.sourceLine: The more man meditates upon good thoughts, the better will be his world and the world at large.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: To attain knowledge, add things every day. To attain wisdom, remove things every day.
items.sourceLine: To attain knowledge, add things every day. To attain wisdom, remove things every day.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: Next week I shall begin my operations on my hat, on which you know my principal hopes of happiness depend.
items.sourceLine: Next week I shall begin my operations on my hat, on which you know my principal hopes of happiness depend.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: What is the good of trying again? You are not the only one—all are alike. Such is life.
items.sourceLine: "Why, you have tried to improve before, and failed," the tempter in his soul whispered. "What is the good of trying again? You are not the only one—all are alike. Such is life." But the free, spiritual being which alone is true, alone powerful, alone eternal, was already awake in Nekhludoff. And he could not help believing it. However great the difference between that which he was and that which he wished to be, for

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: It is better to be unhappy and know the worst, than to be happy in a fool's paradise!
items.sourceLine: It is better to be unhappy and know the worst, than to be happy in a fool's paradise!

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Can words such as Orthodox, Jew, or Catholic really express some sort of exclusive personal virtues or merits?
items.sourceLine: Can words such as Orthodox, Jew, or Catholic really express some sort of exclusive personal virtues or merits?

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The executive of the modern State is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.
items.sourceLine: The executive of the modern State is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Now the Sirens have a still more fatal weapon than their song, namely their silence… Someone might possibly have escaped from their singing; but from their silence, certainly never.
items.sourceLine: Now the Sirens have a still more fatal weapon than their song, namely their silence... Someone might possibly have escaped from their singing; but from their silence, certainly never.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Out of the crooked timber of humanity, no straight thing was ever made.
items.sourceLine: Out of the crooked timber of humanity, no straight thing was ever made.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Is it so big a mystery what god and man and world are? No! but nobody knows how to solve it so the mystery hangs on.
items.sourceLine: Is it so big a mystery what god and man and world are? No! but nobody knows how to solve it so the mystery hangs on.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: We abolished the true world: which world has remained? perhaps the world of appearances?... But no! together with the true world we abolished the world of appearances.
items.sourceLine: Nietzsche's inverted Platonism, his insistence on life and the sensuously and materially given as against the suprasensuous and transcendent ideas which, since Plato, had been supposed to measure, judge, and give meaning to the given, ended in what is commonly called nihilism. Yet Nietzsche was no nihilist but, on the contrary, was the first to try to overcome the nihilism inherent not in the notions of the thinkers

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Christianity taught only what the whole of Asia knew already long before and even better.
items.sourceLine: Christianity taught only what the whole of Asia knew already long before and even better.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: The works of the righteous would be mortal sins if they would not be feared as mortal sins by the righteous themselves out of pious fear of God.
items.sourceLine: The works of the righteous would be mortal sins if they would not be feared as mortal sins by the righteous themselves out of pious fear of God.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: To accede to truth, it suffices that I be any subject that can see what is evident.
items.sourceLine: Descartes, I think, broke with this when he said, "To accede to truth, it suffices that I be any subject that can see what is evident." Evidence is substituted for ascesis at the point where the relationship to the self intersects the relationship to others and the world. The relationship to the self no longer needs to be ascetic to get into relation to the truth. It suffices that the relationship to the self reveals

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Aristotle (…) a mere bond-servant to his logic, thereby rendering it contentious and well nigh useless.
items.sourceLine: Aristotle (...) a mere bond-servant to his logic, thereby rendering it contentious and well nigh useless.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: It's true that there is calm and composure in Spinoza, but surely it's not right to say that that's the whole essence of Spinoza's thought? Surely there's also…

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: Ce miracle de l'Analyse, prodige du monde des idées, objet presque amphibie entre l'Être et le Non-être, que nous appelons racine imaginaire.
items.sourceLine: Ce miracle de l'Analyse, prodige du monde des idées, objet presque amphibie entre l'Être et le Non-être, que nous appelons racine imaginaire.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Generally speaking, the errors in religion are dangerous; those in philosophy only ridiculous.
items.sourceLine: Generally speaking, the errors in religion are dangerous; those in philosophy only ridiculous.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The annual labour of every nation is the fund which originally supplies it with all the necessaries and conveniences of life which it annually consumes.
items.sourceLine: The annual labour of every nation is the fund which originally supplies it with all the necessaries and conveniences of life which it annually consumes.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: The utilitarian doctrine is, that happiness is desirable, and the only thing desirable, as an end; all other things being only desirable as means to that end.
items.sourceLine: The utilitarian doctrine is, that happiness is desirable, and the only thing desirable, as an end; all other things being only desirable as means to that end.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: The moon, too, hid herself Behind the clouds that darkly came over her; High up roarèd the sea, And then triumphantly stood in the heavens The stars all-eternal.
items.sourceLine: The moon, too, hid herself Behind the clouds that darkly came over her; High up roarèd the sea, And then triumphantly stood in the heavens The stars all-eternal.

items.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
items.quote: Es ist unendlich schwer, zu wissen, wenn und wo man bleiben soll, und Tausenden für einen ist das Ziel ihres Nachdenkens die Stelle, wo sie des Nachdenkens müde geworden.
items.sourceLine: Es ist unendlich schwer, zu wissen, wenn und wo man bleiben soll, und Tausenden für einen ist das Ziel ihres Nachdenkens die Stelle, wo sie des Nachdenkens müde geworden.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Inevitably, in the secret chemistry of the emotions the feeling of pity for a sick person is imperceptibly bound up with tenderness.
items.sourceLine: Inevitably, in the secret chemistry of the emotions the feeling of pity for a sick person is imperceptibly bound up with tenderness.

items.author: Dante Alighieri
items.quote: Genus vero philosophie, sub quo hic in toto et parte proceditur, est morale negotium, sive ethica; quia non ad speculandum, sed ad opus inventum est totum et pars.
items.sourceLine: Genus vero philosophie, sub quo hic in toto et parte proceditur, est morale negotium, sive ethica; quia non ad speculandum, sed ad opus inventum est totum et pars.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Gossip is charming! History is merely gossip. But scandal is gossip made tedious by morality.
items.sourceLine: Gossip is charming! History is merely gossip. But scandal is gossip made tedious by morality.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Jésus a pleuré, Voltaire a souri; c’est de cette larme divine et de ce sourire humain qu’est faite la douceur de la civilisation actuelle.
items.sourceLine: Jésus a pleuré, Voltaire a souri; c’est de cette larme divine et de ce sourire humain qu’est faite la douceur de la civilisation actuelle.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Seek first God's Kingdom, that is, become like the lilies and the birds, become perfectly silent — then shall the rest be added unto you.
items.sourceLine: Seek first God's Kingdom, that is, become like the lilies and the birds, become perfectly silent — then shall the rest be added unto you.

items.author: Catherine II of Russia
items.quote: The Usage of Torture is contrary to all the Dictates of Nature and Reason; even Mankind itself cries out against it, and demands loudly the total Abolition of it.
items.section: Proposals for a New Law Code (1768)
items.sourceLine: The Usage of Torture is contrary to all the Dictates of Nature and Reason; even Mankind itself cries out against it, and demands loudly the total Abolition of it.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Let tyrants fear, I have always so behaved myself that, under God, I have placed my chiefest strength and safeguard in the loyal hearts and good-will of my subjects.
items.section: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury (1588)
items.sourceLine: Let tyrants fear, I have always so behaved myself that, under God, I have placed my chiefest strength and safeguard in the loyal hearts and good-will of my subjects.

items.author: Victoria of the United Kingdom
items.quote: It seems to me a defect in our much famed Constitution, to have to part with an admirable Govt like Ld Salisbury's for no question of any importance or any particular reason, merely on account of the number of votes.
items.sourceLine: It seems to me a defect in our much famed Constitution, to have to part with an admirable Govt like Ld Salisbury's for no question of any importance or any particular reason, merely on account of the number of votes.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Ad Graecas literas totum animum applicui; statimque ut pecuniam accepero, Graecos primum autores, deinde vestes emam.
items.sourceLine: Ad Graecas literas totum animum applicui; statimque ut pecuniam accepero, Graecos primum autores, deinde vestes emam.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: The mariner of old said to Neptune in a great tempest, "O God! thou mayest save me if thou wilt, and if thou wilt thou mayest destroy me; but whether or no, I will steer my rudder true.
items.sourceLine: The mariner of old said to Neptune in a great tempest, "O God! thou mayest save me if thou wilt, and if thou wilt thou mayest destroy me; but whether or no, I will steer my rudder true."

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Down in adoration falling, Lo! the sacred Host we hail; Lo! o'er ancient forms departing, Newer rites of grace prevail; Faith for all defects supplying, Where the feeble senses fail.
items.sourceLine: Down in adoration falling, Lo! the sacred Host we hail; Lo! o'er ancient forms departing, Newer rites of grace prevail; Faith for all defects supplying, Where the feeble senses fail.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: The things that are in the world are what God has made. … Why should I not love what God has made?
items.section: Ten Homilies on the First Epistle of John (414)
items.sourceLine: A man might say, "The things that are in the world are what God has made. ... Why should I not love what God has made?" ... Suppose, my brethren, a man should make for his betrothed a ring, and she should prefer the ring given her to the betrothed who made it for her, would not her heart be convicted of infidelity? ... God has given you all these things: therefore, love him who made them.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Must helpless man, in ignorance sedate, Roll darkling down the torrent of his fate?
items.sourceLine: Must helpless man, in ignorance sedate, Roll darkling down the torrent of his fate?

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: One becomes a critic when one cannot be an artist, just as a man becomes a stool pigeon when he cannot be a soldier.
items.sourceLine: One becomes a critic when one cannot be an artist, just as a man becomes a stool pigeon when he cannot be a soldier.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: D'ailleurs, le suicide régnait alors à Paris; ne doit-il pas être le dernier mot des sociétés incrédules?
items.sourceLine: D'ailleurs, le suicide régnait alors à Paris ; ne doit-il pas être le dernier mot des sociétés incrédules ?

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Le scandale du monde est ce qui fait l'offense, Et ce n'est pas pécher que pécher en silence.
items.sourceLine: Le scandale du monde est ce qui fait l'offense, Et ce n'est pas pécher que pécher en silence.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Shakspeare (whom you and every playhouse bill Style the divine! the matchless! what you will), For gain, not glory, wing'd his roving flight, And grew immortal in his own despite.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: Shakspeare (whom you and every playhouse bill Style the divine! the matchless! what you will), For gain, not glory, wing'd his roving flight, And grew immortal in his own despite.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: I'll risk forty dollars that he can outjump any frog in Calaveras county.
items.sourceLine: I'll risk forty dollars that he can outjump any frog in Calaveras county.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: United States! the ages plead, — Present and Past in under-song, — Go put your creed into your deed, Nor speak with double tongue.
items.sourceLine: United States! the ages plead, — Present and Past in under-song, — Go put your creed into your deed, Nor speak with double tongue.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: What are the earth and all its interests beside the deep surmise which pierces and scatters them?
items.sourceLine: What are the earth and all its interests beside the deep surmise which pierces and scatters them?

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Follow the seasons of Ha, Ride in the state carriage of Yau, Wear the ceremonial cap of Chan, Let the music be the Shiu with its pantomimes.
items.sourceLine: Follow the seasons of Ha, Ride in the state carriage of Yau, Wear the ceremonial cap of Chan, Let the music be the Shiu with its pantomimes.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: Block the passages, shut the doors, And till the end your strength shall not fail. Open up the passages, increase your doings, And till your last day no help shall come to you.
items.sourceLine: Block the passages, shut the doors, And till the end your strength shall not fail. Open up the passages, increase your doings, And till your last day no help shall come to you.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.
items.sourceLine: I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: You worldly-minded people are most unfortunate! You are surrounded with sorrows and troubles overhead and underfoot and to the right and to the left, and you are enigmas even to yourselves.
items.sourceLine: You worldly-minded people are most unfortunate! You are surrounded with sorrows and troubles overhead and underfoot and to the right and to the left, and you are enigmas even to yourselves.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: I go to spread the tidings, I want to spread the tidings — of what? Of the truth, for I have seen it, have seen it with my own eyes, have seen it in all its glory.
items.section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)
items.sourceLine: I go to spread the tidings, I want to spread the tidings — of what? Of the truth, for I have seen it, have seen it with my own eyes, have seen it in all its glory.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Is it our job to judge? The gendarme, policemen and bureaucrats have been especially prepared by fate for that job. Our job is to write, and only to write.
items.sourceLine: Is it our job to judge? The gendarme, policemen and bureaucrats have been especially prepared by fate for that job. Our job is to write, and only to write.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: History is not like some individual person, which uses men to achieve its ends. History is nothing but the actions of men in pursuit of their ends.
items.sourceLine: History is not like some individual person, which uses men to achieve its ends. History is nothing but the actions of men in pursuit of their ends.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Als Gregor Samsa eines Morgens aus unruhigen Träumen erwachte, fand er sich in seinem Bett zu einem ungeheuren Ungeziefer verwandelt.
items.sourceLine: Als Gregor Samsa eines Morgens aus unruhigen Träumen erwachte, fand er sich in seinem Bett zu einem ungeheuren Ungeziefer verwandelt.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: …aus so krummem Holze, als woraus der Mensch gemacht ist, kann nichts ganz Gerades gezimmert werden.
items.sourceLine: ...aus so krummem Holze, als woraus der Mensch gemacht ist, kann nichts ganz Gerades gezimmert werden.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Tränenreiche Männer sind gut. Verlasse mich jeder, der trocknen Herzens, trockner Augen ist!
items.sourceLine: Tränenreiche Männer sind gut. Verlasse mich jeder, der trocknen Herzens, trockner Augen ist!

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Who knew that if you merely represent the thought of Nietzsche or Schopenhauer in a fun way it would find such an audience? Some things, it seems, are always green.
items.sourceLine: Who knew that if you merely represent the thought of Nietzsche or Schopenhauer in a fun way it would find such an audience? Some things, it seems, are always green.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Just as the witticism brings two very different real objects under one concept, the pun brings two different concepts, by the assistance of accident, under one word.
items.section: The World as Will and Representation (1819; 1844; 1859)
items.sourceLine: Just as the witticism brings two very different real objects under one concept, the pun brings two different concepts, by the assistance of accident, under one word.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: The mad mob does not ask how it could be better, only that it be different. And when it then becomes worse, it must change again. Thus they get bees for flies, and at last hornets for bees.
items.sourceLine: The mad mob does not ask how it could be better, only that it be different. And when it then becomes worse, it must change again. Thus they get bees for flies, and at last hornets for bees.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: That every individual thing, so far as in it lies, perseveres in the same state, whether of motion or of rest.
items.sourceLine: The primary property of matter was indeed distinctly announced by Descartes in what he calls the "First Law of Nature": "That every individual thing, so far as in it lies, perseveres in the same state, whether of motion or of rest."

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: I bequeath my soul to God (…). My body to be buried obscurely. For my name and memory, I leave it to men's charitable speeches, and to foreign nations, and the next age.
items.sourceLine: I bequeath my soul to God (...). My body to be buried obscurely. For my name and memory, I leave it to men's charitable speeches, and to foreign nations, and the next age.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: How much of personal timidity and vulnerability does this masquerade of a sickly recluse betray!
items.sourceLine: Speaking of Spinoza he [Nietzsche] says: "How much of personal timidity and vulnerability does this masquerade of a sickly recluse betray!" Exactly the same may be said of him, with the less reluctance since he has not hesitated to say it of Spinoza. It is obvious that in his day-dreams he is a warrior, not a professor; all the men he admires were military.

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: Et comme tout présent état d'une substance simple est naturellement une suite de son état précédent, tellement, que le présent y est gros de l'avenir.
items.sourceLine: Et comme tout présent état d'une substance simple est naturellement une suite de son état précédent, tellement, que le présent y est gros de l'avenir.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Grief and disappointment give rise to anger, anger to envy, envy to malice, and malice to grief again, till the whole circle be completed.
items.sourceLine: Grief and disappointment give rise to anger, anger to envy, envy to malice, and malice to grief again, till the whole circle be completed.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Nobody ever saw a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog.
items.sourceLine: Nobody ever saw a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Landlords… grow richer, as it were in their sleep, without working, risking, or economizing.
items.sourceLine: Landlords... grow richer, as it were in their sleep, without working, risking, or economizing.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Ich weiss nicht, was soll es bedeuten, Dass ich so traurig bin; Ein Märchen aus alten Zeiten, Das kommt mir nicht aus dem Sinn.
