items.author: David Hume
items.quote: … no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavors to establish.
items.sourceLine: ... no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavors to establish.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: It is the natural effect of improvement, however, to diminish gradually the real price of almost all manufactures.
items.sourceLine: It is the natural effect of improvement, however, to diminish gradually the real price of almost all manufactures.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Wisdom and contrivance are shown in overcoming difficulties, so there is no place for them in a Being for whom no difficulties exist
items.sourceLine: Wisdom and contrivance are shown in overcoming difficulties, so there is no place for them in a Being for whom no difficulties exist

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Great genius takes shape by contact with another great genius, but less by assimilation than by friction.
items.sourceLine: Great genius takes shape by contact with another great genius, but less by assimilation than by friction.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: If you are going to sell yourself, you should at least get a good price.
items.sourceLine: If you are going to sell yourself, you should at least get a good price.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: The home seems to me to be the proper sphere for the man. And certainly once a man begins to neglect his domestic duties he becomes painfully effeminate, does he not?
items.sourceLine: The home seems to me to be the proper sphere for the man. And certainly once a man begins to neglect his domestic duties he becomes painfully effeminate, does he not?

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: La musique…est la vapeur de l’art. Elle est à la poésie ce que la rêverie est à la pensée, ce que le fluide est au liquide, ce que l’océan des nuées est à l’océan des ondes.
items.sourceLine: La musique...est la vapeur de l’art. Elle est à la poésie ce que la rêverie est à la pensée, ce que le fluide est au liquide, ce que l’océan des nuées est à l’océan des ondes.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Socrates did not stop with a philosophical consideration of mankind; he addressed himself to each one individually, wrested everything from him, and sent him away empty-handed.
items.section: On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates (1841)
items.sourceLine: Socrates did not stop with a philosophical consideration of mankind; he addressed himself to each one individually, wrested everything from him, and sent him away empty-handed.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Those who touch the sceptres of princes deserve no pity.
items.sourceLine: Those who touch the sceptres of princes deserve no pity.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: The worst evil is hardness of heart. Those who do not repent, who deliberately remain in their habits of sin, have the most to fear. p. 146
items.section: The Handbook of the Militant Christian (1514 AD)
items.sourceLine: The worst evil is hardness of heart. Those who do not repent, who deliberately remain in their habits of sin, have the most to fear. p. 146

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: We are, I know not how, double in ourselves, which is the cause that what we believe we do not believe, and cannot disengage ourselves from what we condemn.
items.sourceLine: We are, I know not how, double in ourselves, which is the cause that what we believe we do not believe, and cannot disengage ourselves from what we condemn.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: The highest perfection of human life consists in the mind of man being detached from care, for the sake of God.
items.sourceLine: The highest perfection of human life consists in the mind of man being detached from care, for the sake of God.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Spiritalis enim virtus Sacramenti ita est ut lux: et ab illuminandis pura excipitur, et si per immundos transeat, non inquinatur.
items.sourceLine: Spiritalis enim virtus Sacramenti ita est ut lux: et ab illuminandis pura excipitur, et si per immundos transeat, non inquinatur.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: It is always observable that silence propagates itself, and that the longer talk has been suspended, the more difficult it is to find any thing to say.
items.sourceLine: It is always observable that silence propagates itself, and that the longer talk has been suspended, the more difficult it is to find any thing to say.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: C'était à Mégara, faubourg de Carthage, dans les jardins d'Hamilcar.
items.sourceLine: C'était à Mégara, faubourg de Carthage, dans les jardins d'Hamilcar.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Une jeune fille est comme une fleur qu'on a cueillie; mais la femme coupable est une fleur sur laquelle on a marché.
items.sourceLine: Une jeune fille est comme une fleur qu'on a cueillie ; mais la femme coupable est une fleur sur laquelle on a marché.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Par ma foi, il y a plus de quarante ans que je dis de la prose, sans que j'en susse rien.
items.sourceLine: Par ma foi, il y a plus de quarante ans que je dis de la prose, sans que j'en susse rien.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: If to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been churches, and poor men’s cottages princes’ palaces.
items.sourceLine: If to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been churches, and poor men’s cottages princes’ palaces.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: An experienced, industrious, ambitious, and often quite picturesque liar.
items.sourceLine: An experienced, industrious, ambitious, and often quite picturesque liar.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: What is there in 'Paradise Lost' to elevate and astonish like Herschel or Somerville?
items.sourceLine: What is there in 'Paradise Lost' to elevate and astonish like Herschel or Somerville?

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: The life that I aspire to live No man proposeth me— No trade upon the street Wears its emblazonry.
items.sourceLine: The life that I aspire to live No man proposeth me— No trade upon the street Wears its emblazonry.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Let the states of equilibrium and harmony exist in perfection, and a happy order will prevail throughout heaven and earth, and all things will be nourished and flourish.
items.sourceLine: Let the states of equilibrium and harmony exist in perfection, and a happy order will prevail throughout heaven and earth, and all things will be nourished and flourish.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: He who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.
items.sourceLine: He who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: The pleasures of friendship, of unreserved conversation, of similarity of taste and opinions will make good amends for orange wine.
items.sourceLine: The pleasures of friendship, of unreserved conversation, of similarity of taste and opinions will make good amends for orange wine.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the manifestation of an activity unknown to him, which was his life.
items.sourceLine: He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the manifestation of an activity unknown to him, which was his life.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: To care only for well-being seems to me positively ill-bred. Whether it's good or bad, it is sometimes very pleasant, too, to smash things.
items.sourceLine: To care only for well-being seems to me positively ill-bred. Whether it's good or bad, it is sometimes very pleasant, too, to smash things.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Oh... as though we were thinking of wearing them! They are not to be worn; they are for the trousseau!
items.sourceLine: "My daughter," chanted the little lady, "and, Manetchka, this is a young gentleman who has come," etc. I was introduced, and expressed my surprise at the number of paper patterns. Mother and daughter dropped their eyes. "We had a fair here at Ascension," said the mother; "we always buy materials at the fair, and then it keeps us busy with sewing till the next year's fair comes around again. We never put things out to

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The foundation of irreligious criticism is: Man makes religion, religion does not make man.
items.section: Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1843)
items.sourceLine: The foundation of irreligious criticism is: Man makes religion, religion does not make man.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: The history of mankind is the instant between two strides taken by a traveler.
items.sourceLine: The history of mankind is the instant between two strides taken by a traveler.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: All natural capacities of a creature are destined to evolve completely to their natural end.
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: All natural capacities of a creature are destined to evolve completely to their natural end.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: As great, everlasting, Adamantine laws Dictate, we must all Complete the cycles Of our existence.
items.sourceLine: As great, everlasting, Adamantine laws Dictate, we must all Complete the cycles Of our existence.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: …aesthetischen Sokratismus…dessen oberstes Gesetz ungefähr so lautet: "alles muss verständig sein, um schön zu sein"; als Parallelsatz zu dem sokratischen "nur der Wissende ist tugendhaft.
items.sourceLine: ...aesthetischen Sokratismus...dessen oberstes Gesetz ungefähr so lautet: "alles muss verständig sein, um schön zu sein"; als Parallelsatz zu dem sokratischen "nur der Wissende ist tugendhaft."

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Philosophy of religion … really amounts to … philosophizing on certain favorite assumptions that are not confirmed at all.
items.sourceLine: Philosophy of religion ... really amounts to ... philosophizing on certain favorite assumptions that are not confirmed at all.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: She is rightly called not only the mother of the man, but also the Mother of God … It is certain that Mary is the Mother of the real and true God.
items.sourceLine: "She is rightly called not only the mother of the man, but also the Mother of God ... It is certain that Mary is the Mother of the real and true God.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: His philosophy has long since been superseded by other systems, but the analytical geometry of Descartes will remain a valuable possession forever.
items.sourceLine: His philosophy has long since been superseded by other systems, but the analytical geometry of Descartes will remain a valuable possession forever.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Sacred and inspired divinity, the sabaoth and port of all men's labours and peregrinations.
items.sourceLine: Sacred and inspired divinity, the sabaoth and port of all men's labours and peregrinations.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Spinoza did not seek to found a sect, and he founded none"; yet all philosophy after him is permeated with his thought.
items.sourceLine: "Spinoza did not seek to found a sect, and he founded none"; yet all philosophy after him is permeated with his thought.

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: Ainsi on peut dire que non seulement l'âme, miroir d'un univers indestructible, est indestructible, mais encore l'animal même, quoique sa machine périsse souvent en partie, et quitte ou prenne des dépouilles organiques.
items.sourceLine: Ainsi on peut dire que non seulement l'âme, miroir d'un univers indestructible, est indestructible, mais encore l'animal même, quoique sa machine périsse souvent en partie, et quitte ou prenne des dépouilles organiques.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: He is happy, whose circumstances suit his temper; but he is more excellent, who can suit his temper to any circumstances.
items.section: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals (1751)
items.sourceLine: He is happy, whose circumstances suit his temper; but he is more excellent, who can suit his temper to any circumstances.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: A man must be perfectly crazy who, where there is tolerable security, does not employ all the stock which he commands,…
items.sourceLine: A man must be perfectly crazy who, where there is tolerable security, does not employ all the stock which he commands,...

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: France has done more for even English history than England has.
items.sourceLine: France has done more for even English history than England has.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Oaks shall be rent; the Word shall shatter — Yea, on that fiery day, the Crown, Even the palace walls shall totter, And domes and spires come crashing down.
items.sourceLine: Oaks shall be rent; the Word shall shatter — Yea, on that fiery day, the Crown, Even the palace walls shall totter, And domes and spires come crashing down.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Everything in life that deviates from the straight and, so to speak, normal line, makes people first curious and then indignant.
items.sourceLine: Everything in life that deviates from the straight and, so to speak, normal line, makes people first curious and then indignant.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Oh, I love London society! It is entirely composed now of beautiful idiots and brilliant lunatics. Just what society should be.
items.sourceLine: Oh, I love London society! It is entirely composed now of beautiful idiots and brilliant lunatics. Just what society should be.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Ce qu’on ne peut dire et ce qu’on ne peut taire, la musique l’exprime.
items.sourceLine: Ce qu’on ne peut dire et ce qu’on ne peut taire, la musique l’exprime.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: The world is rejuvenated, but as Heine so wittily remarked, it was rejuvenated by romanticism to such a degree that it became a baby again.
items.section: On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates (1841)
items.sourceLine: The world is rejuvenated, but as Heine so wittily remarked, it was rejuvenated by romanticism to such a degree that it became a baby again.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Anger makes dull men witty, but it keeps them poor.
items.sourceLine: Anger makes dull men witty, but it keeps them poor.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: No Man is wise at all Times, or is without his blind Side.
items.sourceLine: No Man is wise at all Times, or is without his blind Side.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: He who should teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live.
items.sourceLine: He who should teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Now what has been said about the Jews is also to be understood about Cahorsins, and anyone else depending upon the depravity of usury.
items.section: On the Governance of the Jews (c. 1263–1265)
items.sourceLine: Now what has been said about the Jews is also to be understood about Cahorsins, and anyone else depending upon the depravity of usury.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: If thou shouldst say, 'It is enough, I have reached perfection,' all is lost. For it is the function of perfection to make one know one's imperfection.
items.sourceLine: If thou shouldst say, 'It is enough, I have reached perfection,' all is lost. For it is the function of perfection to make one know one's imperfection.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: The reciprocal civility of authors is one of the most risible scenes in the farce of life.
items.sourceLine: The reciprocal civility of authors is one of the most risible scenes in the farce of life.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: Tout le monde, par excès de terreur, devenait brave.
items.sourceLine: Tout le monde, par excès de terreur, devenait brave.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Malheureusement, ce portrait ne corrigera personne de la manie d’aimer de anges au doux sourire, à l’air rêveur, à figure candide, dont le cœur est un coffre-fort.
items.sourceLine: Malheureusement, ce portrait ne corrigera personne de la manie d’aimer de anges au doux sourire, à l’air rêveur, à figure candide, dont le cœur est un coffre-fort.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Ah que je— Vous l'avez voulu, vous l'avez voulu, George Dandin, vous l'avez voulu, cela vous sied fort bien, et vous voilà ajusté comme il faut, vous avez justement ce que vous méritez.
items.sourceLine: Ah que je— Vous l'avez voulu, vous l'avez voulu, George Dandin, vous l'avez voulu, cela vous sied fort bien, et vous voilà ajusté comme il faut, vous avez justement ce que vous méritez.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: The better part of valour is discretion; in the which better part I have saved my life.
items.sourceLine: The better part of valour is discretion; in the which better part I have saved my life.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: All you need in this life is ignorance and confidence, and then Success is sure.
items.sourceLine: All you need in this life is ignorance and confidence, and then Success is sure.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Cure the drunkard, heal the insane, mollify the homicide, civilize the Pawnee, but what lessons can be devised for the debaucher of sentiment?
items.sourceLine: Cure the drunkard, heal the insane, mollify the homicide, civilize the Pawnee, but what lessons can be devised for the debaucher of sentiment?

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: The law will never make men free; it is men who have got to make the law free.
items.sourceLine: The law will never make men free; it is men who have got to make the law free.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: There is no body but eats and drinks. But they are few who can distinguish flavors.
items.sourceLine: There is no body but eats and drinks. But they are few who can distinguish flavors.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: Governing a large country is like frying a small fish.
items.sourceLine: Governing a large country is like frying a small fish.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: I am sorry to tell you that I am getting very extravagant, and spending all my money, and, what is worse for you, I have been spending yours too.
items.sourceLine: I am sorry to tell you that I am getting very extravagant, and spending all my money, and, what is worse for you, I have been spending yours too.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: To love life is to love God. Harder and more blessed than all else is to love this life in one's sufferings, in undeserved sufferings.
items.sourceLine: To love life is to love God. Harder and more blessed than all else is to love this life in one's sufferings, in undeserved sufferings.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: A gentleman, even if he loses everything he owns, must show no emotion. Money must be so far beneath a gentleman that it is hardly worth troubling about.
items.sourceLine: A gentleman, even if he loses everything he owns, must show no emotion. Money must be so far beneath a gentleman that it is hardly worth troubling about.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Ho-ho-ho! This is a fine daughter-in-law for you too! Everything is in its place in her; all runs smoothly, no creaking, the mechanism works well, lots of screws in it.
items.sourceLine: "Grigory Petrovitch, let us weep, let us weep with joy!" he said in a thin voice, and then at once burst out laughing in a loud bass guffaw. "Ho-ho-ho! This is a fine daughter-in-law for you too! Everything is in its place in her; all runs smoothly, no creaking, the mechanism works well, lots of screws in it."

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Every emancipation is a restoration of the human world and of human relationships to a man himself.
items.sourceLine: Every emancipation is a restoration of the human world and of human relationships to a man himself.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: The thornbush is old obstacle in the road. It must catch fire if you want to go further.
items.sourceLine: The thornbush is old obstacle in the road. It must catch fire if you want to go further.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: In man (as the only rational creature on earth) those natural capacities which are directed to the use of his reason are to be fully developed only in the race, not in the individual.
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: In man (as the only rational creature on earth) those natural capacities which are directed to the use of his reason are to be fully developed only in the race, not in the individual.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: He can distinguish, He chooses and judges, He can give permanence To the moment.
items.sourceLine: Only mankind Can do the impossible: He can distinguish, He chooses and judges, He can give permanence To the moment.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Darum hat Lessing, der ehrlichste theoretische Mensch, es auszusprechen gewagt, dass ihm mehr am Suchen der Wahrheit als an ihr selbst gelegen sei…
items.sourceLine: Darum hat Lessing, der ehrlichste theoretische Mensch, es auszusprechen gewagt, dass ihm mehr am Suchen der Wahrheit als an ihr selbst gelegen sei...

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Als auf die große Masse des Menschengeschlechts berechnet und derselben angemessen, kann bloß allegorische Wahrheit enthalten, welche sie jedoch als sensu proprio wahr geltend zu machen hat.
items.sourceLine: Als auf die große Masse des Menschengeschlechts berechnet und derselben angemessen, kann bloß allegorische Wahrheit enthalten, welche sie jedoch als sensu proprio wahr geltend zu machen hat.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: There can be no doubt that the Virgin Mary is in heaven. How it happened we do not know.
items.sourceLine: There can be no doubt that the Virgin Mary is in heaven. How it happened we do not know.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: His Geometry is not easy reading. An edition appeared subsequently with notes by his friend De Beaune, which were intended to remove the difficulties.
items.sourceLine: His Geometry is not easy reading. An edition appeared subsequently with notes by his friend De Beaune, which were intended to remove the difficulties.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Cleanness of body was ever deemed to proceed from a due reverence to God.
items.sourceLine: Cleanness of body was ever deemed to proceed from a due reverence to God.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: I believe in Spinoza's God, who reveals himself in the lawful harmony of the world, not in a God who concerns himself with the fate and the doings of mankind.
items.sourceLine: I believe in Spinoza's God, who reveals himself in the lawful harmony of the world, not in a God who concerns himself with the fate and the doings of mankind.

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: La nature ne fait jamais des sauts.
items.sourceLine: La nature ne fait jamais des sauts.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: During such calm sunshine of the mind, these spectres of false divinity never make their appearance.
items.sourceLine: During such calm sunshine of the mind, these spectres of false divinity never make their appearance.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Though the profusion of Government must undoubtedly have retarded the natural progress of England to wealth and improvement, it has not been able to stop it.
items.sourceLine: Though the profusion of Government must undoubtedly have retarded the natural progress of England to wealth and improvement, it has not been able to stop it.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: The great writers to whom the world owes what religious liberty it possesses, have mostly asserted freedom of conscience as an indefeasible right, and denied absolutely that a human being is accountable to others for his religious belief.
items.sourceLine: The great writers to whom the world owes what religious liberty it possesses, have mostly asserted freedom of conscience as an indefeasible right, and denied absolutely that a human being is accountable to others for his religious belief.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: The music at a wedding procession always reminds me of the music of soldiers going into battle.
items.sourceLine: The music at a wedding procession always reminds me of the music of soldiers going into battle.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: People who are so much at the mercy of their moods should never be given serious responsibilities.
items.sourceLine: People who are so much at the mercy of their moods should never be given serious responsibilities.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Oh, why will parents always appear at the wrong time? Some extraordinary mistake in nature, I suppose.
items.sourceLine: Oh, why will parents always appear at the wrong time? Some extraordinary mistake in nature, I suppose.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: They had done him the honor to take him for a madman, but had set him free on discovering that he was only a poet.
items.sourceLine: They had done him the honor to take him for a madman, but had set him free on discovering that he was only a poet.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Concepts, like individuals, have their histories, and are just as incapable of withstanding the ravages of time as are individuals.
items.section: On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates (1841)
items.sourceLine: Concepts, like individuals, have their histories, and are just as incapable of withstanding the ravages of time as are individuals.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: Kings were wont to honour philosophers, but if I had such I would honour them as angels that should have such piety in them that they would not seek where they are the second to be the first, and where the third to be the second and so forth.
items.sourceLine: Kings were wont to honour philosophers, but if I had such I would honour them as angels that should have such piety in them that they would not seek where they are the second to be the first, and where the third to be the second and so forth.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: I am a lover of liberty. I will not and I cannot serve a party.
items.sourceLine: I am a lover of liberty. I will not and I cannot serve a party.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: All the opinions of the world agree in this, that pleasure is our end.
items.sourceLine: All the opinions of the world agree in this, that pleasure is our end.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Man reaches the highest point of his knowledge about God when he knows that he knows him not, inasmuch as he knows that that which is God transcends whatsoever he conceives of him.
items.sourceLine: Man reaches the highest point of his knowledge about God when he knows that he knows him not, inasmuch as he knows that that which is God transcends whatsoever he conceives of him.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: If there is something more excellent than the truth, then that is God; if not, then truth itself is God.
items.sourceLine: If there is something more excellent than the truth, then that is God; if not, then truth itself is God.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Liberty is, to the lowest rank of every nation, little more than the choice of working or starving.
items.sourceLine: Liberty is, to the lowest rank of every nation, little more than the choice of working or starving.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: What is beautiful is moral, that is all there is to it.
items.sourceLine: What is beautiful is moral, that is all there is to it.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Il y a des femmes dont la grossesse fait sourire quelque célibataire sournois.
items.sourceLine: Il y a des femmes dont la grossesse fait sourire quelque célibataire sournois.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: On ne meurt qu'une fois; et c'est pour si longtemps!
items.sourceLine: On ne meurt qu'une fois; et c'est pour si longtemps!

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Men at some time are masters of their fates: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
items.sourceLine: Men at some time are masters of their fates: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: The difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a large matter—'tis the difference between the lightning-bug and the lightning.
items.sourceLine: The difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a large matter—'tis the difference between the lightning-bug and the lightning.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: He who is in love is wise and is becoming wiser, sees newly every time he looks at the object beloved, drawing from it with his eyes and his mind those virtues which it possesses.
items.sourceLine: He who is in love is wise and is becoming wiser, sees newly every time he looks at the object beloved, drawing from it with his eyes and his mind those virtues which it possesses.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: That virtue we appreciate is as much ours as another's. We see so much only as we possess.
items.sourceLine: That virtue we appreciate is as much ours as another's. We see so much only as we possess.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The superior man accords with the course of the Mean. Though he may be all unknown, unregarded by the world, he feels no regret — It is only the sage who is able for this.
items.sourceLine: The superior man accords with the course of the Mean. Though he may be all unknown, unregarded by the world, he feels no regret — It is only the sage who is able for this.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: A journey of a thousand miles started with a first step.
items.sourceLine: A journey of a thousand miles started with a first step.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: I give you joy of our new nephew, and hope if he ever comes to be hanged it will not be till we are too old to care about it.
items.sourceLine: I give you joy of our new nephew, and hope if he ever comes to be hanged it will not be till we are too old to care about it.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: For us, with the rule of right and wrong given us by Christ, there is nothing for which we have no standard. And there is no greatness where there is not simplicity, goodness, and truth.
items.sourceLine: For us, with the rule of right and wrong given us by Christ, there is nothing for which we have no standard. And there is no greatness where there is not simplicity, goodness, and truth.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Talking nonsense is man's only privilege that distinguishes him from all other organisms.
items.sourceLine: Talking nonsense is man's only privilege that distinguishes him from all other organisms.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Why did you marry me into this family, mother?" said Lipa. "One has to be married, daughter. It was not us who ordained it.
items.sourceLine: "Why did you marry me into this family, mother?" said Lipa. "One has to be married, daughter. It was not us who ordained it."

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Bourgeois society continuously brings forth the Jew from its own entrails.
items.sourceLine: Bourgeois society continuously brings forth the Jew from its own entrails.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: There was once a community of scoundrels, that is to say, they were not scoundrels, but ordinary people.
items.sourceLine: There was once a community of scoundrels, that is to say, they were not scoundrels, but ordinary people.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: The means employed by Nature to bring about the development of all the capacities of men is their antagonism in society, so far as this is, in the end, the cause of a lawful order among men.
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: The means employed by Nature to bring about the development of all the capacities of men is their antagonism in society, so far as this is, in the end, the cause of a lawful order among men.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Only mankind Can do the impossible: He can distinguish, He chooses and judges, He can give permanence To the moment.
items.sourceLine: Only mankind Can do the impossible: He can distinguish, He chooses and judges, He can give permanence To the moment.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Do not forget, man, consumed by lust: you—are the stone, the desert, are death …
items.sourceLine: Do not forget, man, consumed by lust: you—are the stone, the desert, are death ...

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: No doubt, when modesty was made a virtue, it was a very advantageous thing for the fools, for everybody is expected to speak of himself as if he were one.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: No doubt, when modesty was made a virtue, it was a very advantageous thing for the fools, for everybody is expected to speak of himself as if he were one.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: The veneration of Mary is inscribed in the very depths of the human heart.
items.sourceLine: The veneration of Mary is inscribed in the very depths of the human heart.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Do you know who first explained the true origin of the rainbow?
items.sourceLine: "Do you know who first explained the true origin of the rainbow?" I asked. "It was Descartes," he said. After a moment he looked me in the eye. "And what do you think was the salient feature of the rainbow that inspired Descartes' mathematical analysis?" he asked. "Well, the rainbow is actually a section of a cone that appears as an arc of the colors of the spectrum when drops of water are illuminated by sunlight beh

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: They are ill discoverers that think there is no land, when they can see nothing but sea.
items.sourceLine: They are ill discoverers that think there is no land, when they can see nothing but sea.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: I always preferred knowing what an author himself said, to knowing what others thought he ought to have said.
items.sourceLine: Do you remember Goethe's wise words about reading Spinoza? — “I always preferred knowing what an author himself said, to knowing what others thought he ought to have said.”

items.author: Gottfried Leibniz
items.quote: De quelque manière que Dieu aurait créé le monde, il aurait toujours été régulier et dans un certain ordre général. Mais Dieu a choisi celui qui est le plus parfait, c’est-à-dire celui qui est en même temps le plus simple en hypothèses et le plus riche en phénomènes…
items.sourceLine: De quelque manière que Dieu aurait créé le monde, il aurait toujours été régulier et dans un certain ordre général. Mais Dieu a choisi celui qui est le plus parfait, c’est-à-dire celui qui est en même temps le plus simple en hypothèses et le plus riche en phénomènes...

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: A propensity to hope and joy is real riches: One to fear and sorrow, real poverty.
items.sourceLine: A propensity to hope and joy is real riches: One to fear and sorrow, real poverty.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: It seldom happens, however, that a great proprietor is a great improver.
items.sourceLine: It seldom happens, however, that a great proprietor is a great improver.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Truth gains more even by the errors of one who, with due study and preparation, thinks for himself, than by the true opinions of those who only hold them because they do not suffer themselves to think.
items.sourceLine: Truth gains more even by the errors of one who, with due study and preparation, thinks for himself, than by the true opinions of those who only hold them because they do not suffer themselves to think.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: The fundamental evil of the world arose from the fact that the good Lord has not created money enough.
items.sourceLine: The fundamental evil of the world arose from the fact that the good Lord has not created money enough.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: The feeling of self-assurance derived from physical achievement always transfers itself to the mental sphere.
items.sourceLine: The feeling of self-assurance derived from physical achievement always transfers itself to the mental sphere.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Do you really think, Arthur, that it is weakness that yields to temptation? I tell you that there are terrible temptations that it requires strength, strength and courage, to yield to.
items.sourceLine: Do you really think, Arthur, that it is weakness that yields to temptation? I tell you that there are terrible temptations that it requires strength, strength and courage, to yield to.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: It is very fortunate that kings cannot err. Hence their contradictions never perplex us.
items.sourceLine: It is very fortunate that kings cannot err. Hence their contradictions never perplex us.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Irony limits, finitizes, and circumscribes and thereby yields truth, actuality, content; it disciplines and punishes and thereby yields balance and consistency.
items.section: On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates (1841)
items.sourceLine: Irony limits, finitizes, and circumscribes and thereby yields truth, actuality, content; it disciplines and punishes and thereby yields balance and consistency.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: I will make you shorter by the head.
items.sourceLine: I will make you shorter by the head.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Wherever you encounter truth, look upon it as Christianity.
items.sourceLine: Wherever you encounter truth, look upon it as Christianity.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Live as long as you please, you will strike nothing off the time you will have to spend dead.
items.sourceLine: Live as long as you please, you will strike nothing off the time you will have to spend dead.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: There is no order between created being and non-being, but there is between created and uncreated being.
items.sourceLine: There is no order between created being and non-being, but there is between created and uncreated being.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Et illa erant fercula, in quibus mihi esurienti te inferebatur sol et luna.
items.sourceLine: Et illa erant fercula, in quibus mihi esurienti te inferebatur sol et luna.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Nature has given women so much power that the law has very wisely given them little.
items.sourceLine: Nature has given women so much power that the law has very wisely given them little.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: There is no 'true'. There are merely ways of perceiving truth.
items.sourceLine: There is no 'true'. There are merely ways of perceiving truth.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Les femmes les plus vertueuses ont en elles quelque chose qui n'est jamais chaste.
items.sourceLine: Les femmes les plus vertueuses ont en elles quelque chose qui n'est jamais chaste.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?
items.sourceLine: Que diable allait-il faire dans cette galère?

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
items.sourceLine: Men at some time are masters of their fates: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Weather is a literary specialty, and no untrained hand can turn out a good article on it.
items.sourceLine: Weather is a literary specialty, and no untrained hand can turn out a good article on it.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: I fancy I need more than another to speak (rather than write), with such a formidable tendency to the lapidary style. I build my house of boulders.
items.sourceLine: I fancy I need more than another to speak (rather than write), with such a formidable tendency to the lapidary style. I build my house of boulders.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: We are as much as we see. Faith is sight and knowledge. The hands only serve the eyes.
items.sourceLine: We are as much as we see. Faith is sight and knowledge. The hands only serve the eyes.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The way of the superior man may be found, in its simple elements, in the intercourse of common men and women; but in its utmost reaches, it shines brightly through Heaven and Earth.
items.sourceLine: The way of the superior man may be found, in its simple elements, in the intercourse of common men and women; but in its utmost reaches, it shines brightly through Heaven and Earth.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: A thousand-mile journey starts from your feet down there.
items.sourceLine: A thousand-mile journey starts from your feet down there.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: I will not say that your mulberry-trees are dead, but I am afraid they are not alive.
items.sourceLine: I will not say that your mulberry-trees are dead, but I am afraid they are not alive.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To seize and put into words, to describe directly the life of humanity or even of a single nation, appears impossible.
items.sourceLine: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To seize and put into words, to describe directly the life of humanity or even of a single nation, appears impossible.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Accept suffering and achieve atonement through it — that is what you must do.
items.sourceLine: Accept suffering and achieve atonement through it — that is what you must do.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Dear and most respected bookcase! I welcome your existence, which has for over one hundred years been devoted to the radiant ideals of goodness and justice.
items.sourceLine: Dear and most respected bookcase! I welcome your existence, which has for over one hundred years been devoted to the radiant ideals of goodness and justice.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Der Philosoph legt sich – also selbst eine abstrakte Gestalt des entfremdeten Menschen – als den Maßstab der entfremdeten Welt an.
items.sourceLine: Der Philosoph legt sich – also selbst eine abstrakte Gestalt des entfremdeten Menschen – als den Maßstab der entfremdeten Welt an.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Anyone who believes cannot experience miracles. By day one does not see any stars. Anyone who does miracles says: I cannot let go of the earth.
items.sourceLine: Anyone who believes cannot experience miracles. By day one does not see any stars. Anyone who does miracles says: I cannot let go of the earth.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: The greatest problem for the human race, to the solution of which Nature drives man, is the achievement of a universal civic society which administers law among men.
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: The greatest problem for the human race, to the solution of which Nature drives man, is the achievement of a universal civic society which administers law among men.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Let the noble man Be generous and good, Tirelessly achieving What is just and useful: Let him be a model For those beings whom he surmises.
items.sourceLine: Let the noble man Be generous and good, Tirelessly achieving What is just and useful: Let him be a model For those beings whom he surmises.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: There is nothing to life that has value, except the degree of power—assuming that life itself is the will to power.
items.sourceLine: There is nothing to life that has value, except the degree of power—assuming that life itself is the will to power.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Ruhm muß daher erst erworben werden: die Ehre hingegen braucht bloß nicht verloren zu gehen.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: Ruhm muß daher erst erworben werden: die Ehre hingegen braucht bloß nicht verloren zu gehen.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: God has formed the soul and body of the Virgin Mary full of the Holy Spirit, so that she is without all sins, for she has conceived and borne the Lord Jesus.
items.sourceLine: God has formed the soul and body of the Virgin Mary full of the Holy Spirit, so that she is without all sins, for she has conceived and borne the Lord Jesus.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Okay, I give up. What would you say inspired his theory?
items.sourceLine: "Do you know who first explained the true origin of the rainbow?" I asked. "It was Descartes," he said. After a moment he looked me in the eye. "And what do you think was the salient feature of the rainbow that inspired Descartes' mathematical analysis?" he asked. "Well, the rainbow is actually a section of a cone that appears as an arc of the colors of the spectrum when drops of water are illuminated by sunlight beh

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: But men must know that in this theater of man's life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.
items.sourceLine: But men must know that in this theater of man's life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Spinoza is the originator of speculative philosophy, Schelling its restorer, Hegel its perfecter.
items.sourceLine: Spinoza is the originator of speculative philosophy, Schelling its restorer, Hegel its perfecter.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: As to the Approbation or Esteem of those Blockheads who call themselves the Public, & whom a Bookseller, a Lord, a Priest, or a Party can guide, I do most heartily despise it.
items.sourceLine: As to the Approbation or Esteem of those Blockheads who call themselves the Public, & whom a Bookseller, a Lord, a Priest, or a Party can guide, I do most heartily despise it.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: A merchant, it has been said very properly, is not necessarily the citizen of any particular country.
items.sourceLine: A merchant, it has been said very properly, is not necessarily the citizen of any particular country.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: For my own part, not believing in universal selfishness, I have no difficulty in admitting that Communism would even now be practicable among the elite of mankind, and may become so among the rest.
items.sourceLine: For my own part, not believing in universal selfishness, I have no difficulty in admitting that Communism would even now be practicable among the elite of mankind, and may become so among the rest.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: My songs, they say, are poisoned. How else, love, could it be? Thou hast, with deadly magic, Poured poison into me.
items.sourceLine: My songs, they say, are poisoned. How else, love, could it be? Thou hast, with deadly magic, Poured poison into me.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: A man of limited vision is hard to bear with in any sphere in which he is invested with power, but intolerable in the army.
items.sourceLine: A man of limited vision is hard to bear with in any sphere in which he is invested with power, but intolerable in the army.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: When one has weighed the sun in the balance, and measured the steps of the moon, and mapped out the seven heavens, there still remains oneself. Who can calculate the orbit of his own soul?
items.sourceLine: When one has weighed the sun in the balance, and measured the steps of the moon, and mapped out the seven heavens, there still remains oneself. Who can calculate the orbit of his own soul?

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Mettre tout en équilibre, c'est bien; mettre tout en harmonie, c'est mieux.
items.sourceLine: Mettre tout en équilibre, c'est bien; mettre tout en harmonie, c'est mieux.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Old age realizes the dreams of youth: look at Dean Swift; in his youth he built an asylum for the insane, in his old age he was himself an inmate.
items.sourceLine: Old age realizes the dreams of youth: look at Dean Swift; in his youth he built an asylum for the insane, in his old age he was himself an inmate.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: I know I have the body but of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm.
items.section: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury (1588)
items.sourceLine: I know I have the body but of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: I am a citizen of the world, known to all and to all a stranger.
items.sourceLine: I am a citizen of the world, known to all and to all a stranger.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: The laws of conscience, which we pretend to be derived from nature, proceed from custom.
items.sourceLine: The laws of conscience, which we pretend to be derived from nature, proceed from custom.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Vita enim in hoc maxime manifestatur quod aliquid movet se ipsum; quod autem non potest moveri nisi ab alio, quasi mortuum esse videtur.
items.section: On The Perfection of the Spiritual Life (1269-1270)
items.sourceLine: Vita enim in hoc maxime manifestatur quod aliquid movet se ipsum; quod autem non potest moveri nisi ab alio, quasi mortuum esse videtur.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: At ego adulescens miser ualde, miser in exordio ipsius adulescentiae, etiam petieram a te castitatem et dixeram, 'Da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo.
items.sourceLine: At ego adulescens miser ualde, miser in exordio ipsius adulescentiae, etiam petieram a te castitatem et dixeram, 'Da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Resolve to spend a certain number of hours every day amongst your books.
items.sourceLine: Resolve to spend a certain number of hours every day amongst your books.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: Notre ignorance de l'histoire nous fait calomnier notre temps.
items.sourceLine: Notre ignorance de l'histoire nous fait calomnier notre temps.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Un homme ne peut se marier sans avoir étudié l'anatomie et disséqué une femme au moins.
items.sourceLine: Un homme ne peut se marier sans avoir étudié l'anatomie et disséqué une femme au moins.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Tirer les marrons du feu avec la patte du chat.
items.sourceLine: Tirer les marrons du feu avec la patte du chat.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts.
items.sourceLine: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: I am opposed to millionaires, but it would be dangerous to offer me the position.
items.sourceLine: I am opposed to millionaires, but it would be dangerous to offer me the position.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Yet a man may love a paradox, without losing either his wit or his honesty.
items.sourceLine: Yet a man may love a paradox, without losing either his wit or his honesty.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: A slight sound at evening lifts me up by the ears, and makes life seem inexpressibly serene and grand. It may be Uranus, or it may be in the shutter.
items.sourceLine: A slight sound at evening lifts me up by the ears, and makes life seem inexpressibly serene and grand. It may be Uranus, or it may be in the shutter.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The Path is not far from man. When men try to pursue a course, which is far from the common indications of consciousness, this course cannot be considered The Path.
items.sourceLine: The Path is not far from man. When men try to pursue a course, which is far from the common indications of consciousness, this course cannot be considered The Path.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: When men lack a sense of awe, there will be disaster.
items.sourceLine: When men lack a sense of awe, there will be disaster.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: Mr. Digweed has used us basely. Handsome is as handsome does; he is therefore a very ill-looking man.
items.sourceLine: Mr. Digweed has used us basely. Handsome is as handsome does; he is therefore a very ill-looking man.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Все счастливые семьи похожи друг на друга, каждая несчастливая семья несчастлива по-своему.
items.sourceLine: Все счастливые семьи похожи друг на друга, каждая несчастливая семья несчастлива по-своему.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart. The really great men must, I think, have great sadness on Earth.
items.sourceLine: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart. The really great men must, I think, have great sadness on Earth.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: The cherry orchard is now mine!… I bought the estate on which my grandfather and father were slaves, where they were not even permitted in the kitchen.
items.sourceLine: The cherry orchard is now mine!... I bought the estate on which my grandfather and father were slaves, where they were not even permitted in the kitchen.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The product of labour is labour which has been congealed in an object, which has become material: it is the objectification of labour. Labour's realization is its objectification.
items.sourceLine: The product of labour is labour which has been congealed in an object, which has become material: it is the objectification of labour. Labour's realization is its objectification.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Das Böse weiß vom Guten, aber das Gute vom Bösen nicht. Selbsterkenntnis hat nur das Böse.
items.sourceLine: Das Böse weiß vom Guten, aber das Gute vom Bösen nicht. Selbsterkenntnis hat nur das Böse. - Die Acht Oktavhefte; published by BookRix, 9-8-2014.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: This problem is the most difficult and the last to be solved by mankind.
items.section: Idea for a Universal History from a Cosmopolitan Point of View (1784)
items.sourceLine: This problem is the most difficult and the last to be solved by mankind.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: A noble person attracts noble people, and knows how to hold on to them.
items.sourceLine: A noble person attracts noble people, and knows how to hold on to them.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: This is the antinomy: Insofar as we believe in morality we pass sentence on existence.
items.sourceLine: This is the antinomy: Insofar as we believe in morality we pass sentence on existence.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: A reproach can only hurt if it hits the mark. Whoever knows that he does not deserve a reproach can treat it with contempt.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: A reproach can only hurt if it hits the mark. Whoever knows that he does not deserve a reproach can treat it with contempt.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: I cannot forbid a person to marry several wives, for it does not contradict Scripture.
items.sourceLine: I cannot forbid a person to marry several wives, for it does not contradict Scripture.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Le bon sens est la chose du monde la mieux partagée: car chacun pense en être si bien pourvu, que ceux même qui sont les plus difficiles à contenter en toute autre chose, n'ont point coutume d'en désirer plus qu'ils en ont.
items.sourceLine: Le bon sens est la chose du monde la mieux partagée : car chacun pense en être si bien pourvu, que ceux même qui sont les plus difficiles à contenter en toute autre chose, n'ont point coutume d'en désirer plus qu'ils en ont.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: We are much beholden to Machiavel and others, that write what men do, and not what they ought to do.
items.sourceLine: We are much beholden to Machiavel and others, that write what men do, and not what they ought to do.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Spinoza helps me to see myself objectively. This makes life bearable even in experiencing suffering; and with the teachings from the Ethics the world is perceived as manageable.
items.sourceLine: Spinoza helps me to see myself objectively. This makes life bearable even in experiencing suffering; and with the teachings from the Ethics the world is perceived as manageable.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: This avidity alone, of acquiring goods and possessions for ourselves and our nearest friends, is insatiable, perpetual, universal, and directly destructive of society.
items.sourceLine: This avidity alone, of acquiring goods and possessions for ourselves and our nearest friends, is insatiable, perpetual, universal, and directly destructive of society.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: All for ourselves, and nothing for other people, seems, in every age of the world, to have been the vile maxim of the masters of mankind.
items.sourceLine: All for ourselves, and nothing for other people, seems, in every age of the world, to have been the vile maxim of the masters of mankind.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: A bureaucracy always tends to become a pedantocracy.
items.sourceLine: A bureaucracy always tends to become a pedantocracy.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Darling maiden, who can be Ever found to equal thee? To thy service joyfully Shall my life be pledged by me. Thy sweet eyes gleam tenderly, Like soft moonbeams o’er the sea; Lights of rosy harmony O’er thy red cheeks wander free.
items.sourceLine: Darling maiden, who can be Ever found to equal thee? To thy service joyfully Shall my life be pledged by me. Thy sweet eyes gleam tenderly, Like soft moonbeams o’er the sea; Lights of rosy harmony O’er thy red cheeks wander free.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: The heart is able to bury deep and well what is urgently desires to forget.
items.sourceLine: The heart is able to bury deep and well what is urgently desires to forget.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: It is sweet to dance to violins When Love and Life are fair: To dance to flutes, to dance to lutes Is delicate and rare: But it is not sweet with nimble feet To dance upon the air!
items.sourceLine: It is sweet to dance to violins When Love and Life are fair: To dance to flutes, to dance to lutes Is delicate and rare: But it is not sweet with nimble feet To dance upon the air!

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: En somme, je fais ce que je peux, je souffre de la souffrance universelle, et je tâche de la soulager, je n'ai que les chétives forces d'un homme, et je crie à tous: aidez-moi.
items.section: Letter To M. Daelli on Les Misérables (1862)
items.sourceLine: En somme, je fais ce que je peux, je souffre de la souffrance universelle, et je tâche de la soulager, je n'ai que les chétives forces d'un homme, et je crie à tous: aidez-moi.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Most men pursue pleasure with such breathless haste that they hurry past it.
items.sourceLine: Most men pursue pleasure with such breathless haste that they hurry past it.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.
items.sourceLine: If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Whatever you see in the more material part of yourself, learn to refer to God and to the invisible part of yourself. In that way, whatever offers itself to the senses will become for you an occasion for the practice of piety.
items.sourceLine: Whatever you see in the more material part of yourself, learn to refer to God and to the invisible part of yourself. In that way, whatever offers itself to the senses will become for you an occasion for the practice of piety.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: We must not attach knowledge to the mind, we have to incorporate it there.
items.sourceLine: We must not attach knowledge to the mind, we have to incorporate it there.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Tria sunt homini necessaria ad salutem: scilicit scientia credendorum, scientia desiderandorum, et scientia operandorum.
items.sourceLine: Tria sunt homini necessaria ad salutem: scilicit scientia credendorum, scientia desiderandorum, et scientia operandorum.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Deus, dona hominibus videre in parvo communes notitias rerum parvarum atque magnarum.
items.sourceLine: Deus, dona hominibus videre in parvo communes notitias rerum parvarum atque magnarum.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: I have always suspected that the reading is right, which requires many words to prove it wrong; and the emendation wrong, that cannot without so much labour appear to be right.
items.sourceLine: I have always suspected that the reading is right, which requires many words to prove it wrong; and the emendation wrong, that cannot without so much labour appear to be right.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: J'ai eu, aussi, moi, mon époque nerveuse, mon époque sentimentale, et j'en porte encore, comme un galérien, la marque au cou. Avec ma main brûlée j'ai le droit maintenant d'écrire des phrases sur la nature du feu.
items.sourceLine: J'ai eu, aussi, moi, mon époque nerveuse, mon époque sentimentale, et j'en porte encore, comme un galérien, la marque au cou. Avec ma main brûlée j'ai le droit maintenant d'écrire des phrases sur la nature du feu.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: La puissance ne consiste pas à frapper fort ou souvent, mais à frapper juste.
items.sourceLine: La puissance ne consiste pas à frapper fort ou souvent, mais à frapper juste.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Le monde, chère Agnès, est une étrange chose.
items.sourceLine: Le monde, chère Agnès, est une étrange chose.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts.
items.sourceLine: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: A round man cannot be expected to fit in a square hole right away. He must have time to modify his shape.
items.sourceLine: A round man cannot be expected to fit in a square hole right away. He must have time to modify his shape.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Literature is the effort of man to indemnify himself for the wrongs of his condition.
items.sourceLine: Literature is the effort of man to indemnify himself for the wrongs of his condition.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: And the cost of a thing it will be remembered as the amount of life it requires to be exchanged for it.
items.sourceLine: And the cost of a thing it will be remembered as the amount of life it requires to be exchanged for it.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The superior man governs men, according to their nature, with what is proper to them, and as soon as they change what is wrong, he stops.
items.sourceLine: The superior man governs men, according to their nature, with what is proper to them, and as soon as they change what is wrong, he stops.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: People starved because the ruler taxed too heavily.
items.sourceLine: People starved because the ruler taxed too heavily.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: Let me know when you begin the new tea, and the new white wine. My present elegancies have not yet made me indifferent to such matters. I am still a cat if I see a mouse.
items.sourceLine: Let me know when you begin the new tea, and the new white wine. My present elegancies have not yet made me indifferent to such matters. I am still a cat if I see a mouse.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: It's an utterly different culture—their culture. He's cultivated, one sees, simply to be able to despise culture, as they despise everything but animal pleasures.
items.sourceLine: "If you want him defined, here he is: a prime, well-fed beast such as takes medals at the cattle shows, and nothing more," he said, with a tone of vexation that interested her. "No; how so?" she replied. "He's seen a great deal, anyway; he's cultured?" "It's an utterly different culture—their culture. He's cultivated, one sees, simply to be able to despise culture, as they despise everything but animal pleasures."

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: The more cunning a man is, the less he suspects that he will be caught in a simple thing. The more cunning a man is, the simpler the trap he must be caught in.
items.sourceLine: The more cunning a man is, the less he suspects that he will be caught in a simple thing. The more cunning a man is, the simpler the trap he must be caught in.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: We live not in order to eat, but in order not to know what we feel like eating.
items.sourceLine: We live not in order to eat, but in order not to know what we feel like eating.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Manufacture was all the time sheltered by protective duties in the hoe market, by monopolies in the colonial market, and broad as much as possible by differential duties.
items.sourceLine: Manufacture was all the time sheltered by protective duties in the hoe market, by monopolies in the colonial market, and broad as much as possible by differential duties.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: What is meant by its nature for the highest and the best, spreads among the lowly people.
items.sourceLine: What is meant by its nature for the highest and the best, spreads among the lowly people.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Es ist überall nichts in der Welt, ja überhaupt auch außer derselben zu denken möglich, was ohne Einschränkung für gut könnte gehalten werden, als allein ein guter Wille.
items.section: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)
items.sourceLine: Es ist überall nichts in der Welt, ja überhaupt auch außer derselben zu denken möglich, was ohne Einschränkung für gut könnte gehalten werden, als allein ein guter Wille.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: One of the most striking signs of the decay of art is the intermixing of different genres.
items.sourceLine: One of the most striking signs of the decay of art is the intermixing of different genres.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: A man as he ought to be: that sounds to us as insipid as "a tree as it ought to be.
items.sourceLine: A man as he ought to be: that sounds to us as insipid as "a tree as it ought to be."

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: The brain may be regarded as a kind of parasite of the organism, a pensioner, as it were, who dwells with the body.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: The brain may be regarded as a kind of parasite of the organism, a pensioner, as it were, who dwells with the body.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: …women and girls begin to bare themselves behind and in front, and there is nobody to punish and hold in check, and besides, God’s word is mocked.
items.sourceLine: ...women and girls begin to bare themselves behind and in front, and there is nobody to punish and hold in check, and besides, God’s word is mocked.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Descartes was an eminent mathematician, and it would seem that the bent of his mind led him to overestimate the value of deductive reasoning from general principles, as much as Bacon had underestimated it.
items.sourceLine: Descartes was an eminent mathematician, and it would seem that the bent of his mind led him to overestimate the value of deductive reasoning from general principles, as much as Bacon had underestimated it.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: For the inquisition of Final Causes is barren, and like a virgin consecrated to God produces nothing.
items.sourceLine: For the inquisition of Final Causes is barren, and like a virgin consecrated to God produces nothing.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Spinoza: the absolute philosopher, whose Ethics is the foremost book on concepts.
items.sourceLine: Spinoza: the absolute philosopher, whose Ethics is the foremost book on concepts.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Does a man of sense run after every silly tale of hobgoblins or fairies, and canvass particularly the evidence? I never knew anyone, that examined and deliberated about nonsense who did not believe it before the end of his enquiries.
items.sourceLine: Does a man of sense run after every silly tale of hobgoblins or fairies, and canvass particularly the evidence? I never knew anyone, that examined and deliberated about nonsense who did not believe it before the end of his enquiries.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: When the profits of trade happen to be greater than ordinary, over-trading becomes a general error both among great and small dealers.
items.sourceLine: When the profits of trade happen to be greater than ordinary, over-trading becomes a general error both among great and small dealers.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Among a people without fellow-feeling, especially if they read and speak different languages, the united public opinion, necessary to the working of the representative government, cannot exist.
items.sourceLine: Among a people without fellow-feeling, especially if they read and speak different languages, the united public opinion, necessary to the working of the representative government, cannot exist.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: At first I was almost about to despair, I thought I never could bear it
items.sourceLine: At first I was almost about to despair, I thought I never could bear it — but I did bear it. The question remains: how?

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: For one who is having no personal experience, the passionate disquiet of others is at any rate a titillation of the nerves, like seeing a play or listening to music.
items.section: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Woman (1927)
items.sourceLine: For one who is having no personal experience, the passionate disquiet of others is at any rate a titillation of the nerves, like seeing a play or listening to music.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: To dance to flutes, to dance to lutes Is delicate and rare: But it is not sweet with nimble feet To dance upon the air!
items.sourceLine: It is sweet to dance to violins When Love and Life are fair: To dance to flutes, to dance to lutes Is delicate and rare: But it is not sweet with nimble feet To dance upon the air!

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Ces deux moitiés de Dieu, le pape et l'empereur!
items.sourceLine: Ces deux moitiés de Dieu, le pape et l'empereur!

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: If the ethical – that is, social morality – is the highest … then no categories are needed other than the Greek philosophical categories.
items.sourceLine: If the ethical – that is, social morality – is the highest ... then no categories are needed other than the Greek philosophical categories.

items.author: Elizabeth I of England
items.quote: And whereas you would frighten us, by telling how emperors, kings, and princes have owned the bishop of Rome's authority; it was contrary in the beginning. For our Saviour Christ paid his tribute unto Caesar, as the chief superior; which shews your Romish supremacy is usurped.
items.sourceLine: And whereas you would frighten us, by telling how emperors, kings, and princes have owned the bishop of Rome's authority; it was contrary in the beginning. For our Saviour Christ paid his tribute unto Caesar, as the chief superior; which shews your Romish supremacy is usurped.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Once we have tasted the sweetness of what is spiritual, the pleasures of the world will have no attraction for us. If we disregard the shadows of things, then we will penetrate their inner substance.
items.section: The Handbook of the Militant Christian (1514 AD)
items.sourceLine: Once we have tasted the sweetness of what is spiritual, the pleasures of the world will have no attraction for us. If we disregard the shadows of things, then we will penetrate their inner substance.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Every other knowledge is harmful to him who does not have knowledge of goodness.
items.sourceLine: Every other knowledge is harmful to him who does not have knowledge of goodness.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Now, as the Word of God is the Son of God, so the love of God is the Holy Spirit.
items.sourceLine: Now, as the Word of God is the Son of God, so the love of God is the Holy Spirit.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Thus, in this universal catastrophe, the sufferings of Christians have tended to their moral improvement, because they viewed them with eyes of faith.
items.sourceLine: Thus, in this universal catastrophe, the sufferings of Christians have tended to their moral improvement, because they viewed them with eyes of faith.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: The only end of writing is to enable the readers better to enjoy life, or better to endure it.
items.sourceLine: The only end of writing is to enable the readers better to enjoy life, or better to endure it.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: Don't talk to me about your hideous reality! What does it mean
items.sourceLine: Don't talk to me about your hideous reality! What does it mean — reality? Some see things black, others blue — the multitude sees them brute-fashion. There is nothing less natural than Michael Angelo; there is nothing more powerful!
