items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Il est plus facile d'être amant que mari, par la raison qu'il est plus difficile d'avoir de l'esprit tous les jours que de dire de jolies choses de temps en temps.
items.sourceLine: Il est plus facile d'être amant que mari, par la raison qu'il est plus difficile d'avoir de l'esprit tous les jours que de dire de jolies choses de temps en temps.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Une femme d'esprit est un diable en intrigue.
items.sourceLine: Une femme d'esprit est un diable en intrigue.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.
items.sourceLine: 'The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.'

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Humor is the great thing, the saving thing. The minute it crops up, all our hardnesses yield, all our irritations and resentments flit away and a sunny spirit takes their place.
items.sourceLine: Humor is the great thing, the saving thing. The minute it crops up, all our hardnesses yield, all our irritations and resentments flit away and a sunny spirit takes their place.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: Poetry teaches the enormous force of a few words, and, in proportion to the inspiration, checks loquacity.
items.sourceLine: Poetry teaches the enormous force of a few words, and, in proportion to the inspiration, checks loquacity.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms, and did my duty faithfully, though I never received one cent for it.
items.sourceLine: For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms, and did my duty faithfully, though I never received one cent for it.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: To be fond of learning is to be near to knowledge. To practice with vigor is to be near to magnanimity. To possess the feeling of shame is to be near to energy.
items.sourceLine: To be fond of learning is to be near to knowledge. To practice with vigor is to be near to magnanimity. To possess the feeling of shame is to be near to energy.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: The more prohibitions that are imposed on people, The poorer the people become. The more laws and regulations that exist, The more thieves and brigands appear. The more laws and order are made prominent, the more thieves and robbers there will be.
items.sourceLine: The more prohibitions that are imposed on people, The poorer the people become. The more laws and regulations that exist, The more thieves and brigands appear. The more laws and order are made prominent, the more thieves and robbers there will be.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: By the bye, as I must leave off being young, I find many douceurs in being a sort of chaperon, for I am put on the sofa near the fire and can drink as much wine as I like.
items.sourceLine: By the bye, as I must leave off being young, I find many douceurs in being a sort of chaperon, for I am put on the sofa near the fire and can drink as much wine as I like.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: There is one evident, indubitable manifestation of the Divinity, and that is the laws of right which are made known to the world through Revelation.
items.sourceLine: There is one evident, indubitable manifestation of the Divinity, and that is the laws of right which are made known to the world through Revelation.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Your worst sin is that you have destroyed and betrayed yourself for nothing.
items.sourceLine: Your worst sin is that you have destroyed and betrayed yourself for nothing.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: If only one tooth aches, rejoice that not all of them ache…. If your wife betrays you, be glad that she betrayed only you and not the nation.
items.sourceLine: If only one tooth aches, rejoice that not all of them ache.... If your wife betrays you, be glad that she betrayed only you and not the nation.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Nicht das Bewußtsein bestimmt das Leben, sondern das Leben bestimmt das Bewußtsein.
items.sourceLine: Nicht das Bewußtsein bestimmt das Leben, sondern das Leben bestimmt das Bewußtsein.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Everything you say is boring and incomprehensible," she said, "but that alone doesn't make it true.
items.sourceLine: "Everything you say is boring and incomprehensible," she said, "but that alone doesn't make it true."

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Ich soll niemals anders verfahren als so, dass ich auch wollen könne, meine Maxime solle ein allgemeines Gesetz werden.
items.section: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)
items.sourceLine: Ich soll niemals anders verfahren als so, dass ich auch wollen könne, meine Maxime solle ein allgemeines Gesetz werden.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: In limitations he first shows himself the master, And the law can only bring us freedom.
items.sourceLine: In limitations he first shows himself the master, And the law can only bring us freedom.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: No more fiction for us: we calculate; but that we may calculate, we had to make fiction first.
items.sourceLine: No more fiction for us: we calculate; but that we may calculate, we had to make fiction first.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Alles, alles kann einer vergessen, nur nicht sich selbst, sein eigenes Wesen.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: Alles, alles kann einer vergessen, nur nicht sich selbst, sein eigenes Wesen.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: The First Sermon on the Day of the Visitation of Mary (Die erste Predigt am Tag der Heimsuchung Mariä). (1532).
items.sourceLine: The First Sermon on the Day of the Visitation of Mary (Die erste Predigt am Tag der Heimsuchung Mariä). (1532).

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: The primary property of matter was indeed distinctly announced by Descartes in what he calls the "First Law of Nature": "That every individual thing, so far as in it lies, perseveres in the same state, whether of motion or of rest.
items.sourceLine: The primary property of matter was indeed distinctly announced by Descartes in what he calls the "First Law of Nature": "That every individual thing, so far as in it lies, perseveres in the same state, whether of motion or of rest."

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: It would be an unsound fancy and self-contradictory to expect that things which have never yet been done can be done except by means which have never yet been tried.
items.sourceLine: It would be an unsound fancy and self-contradictory to expect that things which have never yet been done can be done except by means which have never yet been tried.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Spinoza is the Christ of philosophers, and the greatest philosophers are hardly more than apostles who distance themselves from or draw near to this mystery.
items.sourceLine: Spinoza is the Christ of philosophers, and the greatest philosophers are hardly more than apostles who distance themselves from or draw near to this mystery.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Here am I who have written on all sorts of subjects calculated to excite hostility, moral, political, and religious, and yet I have no enemies
items.sourceLine: Here am I who have written on all sorts of subjects calculated to excite hostility, moral, political, and religious, and yet I have no enemies — except, indeed, all the Whigs, all the Tories, and all the Christians.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Goods can serve many other purposes besides purchasing money, but money can serve no other purpose besides purchasing goods.
items.sourceLine: Goods can serve many other purposes besides purchasing money, but money can serve no other purpose besides purchasing goods.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: It is also a study peculiarly adapted to an early stage in the education of philosophical students, since it does not presuppose the slow process of acquiring, by experience and reflection, valuable thoughts of their own.
items.sourceLine: It is also a study peculiarly adapted to an early stage in the education of philosophical students, since it does not presuppose the slow process of acquiring, by experience and reflection, valuable thoughts of their own.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: So we keep asking, over and over, Until a handful of earth Stops our mouths
items.sourceLine: So we keep asking, over and over, Until a handful of earth Stops our mouths — But is that an answer?

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: He who studies without passion will never become anything more than a pedant. We must approach knowledge from the inside; inspired by passion.
items.section: Confusion of Feelings or Confusion: The Private Papers of Privy Councillor R. Von D (1927)
items.sourceLine: He who studies without passion will never become anything more than a pedant. We must approach knowledge from the inside; inspired by passion.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: For Man's grim Justice goes its way, And will not swerve aside: It slays the weak, it slays the strong, It has a deadly stride: With iron heel it slays the strong, The monstrous parricide!
items.sourceLine: For Man's grim Justice goes its way, And will not swerve aside: It slays the weak, it slays the strong, It has a deadly stride: With iron heel it slays the strong, The monstrous parricide!

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Dieu s'est fait homme; soit. Le diable s'est fait femme!
items.sourceLine: Dieu s'est fait homme; soit. Le diable s'est fait femme!

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: The question is asked in ignorance, by one who does not even know what can have led him to ask it.
items.sourceLine: The question is asked in ignorance, by one who does not even know what can have led him to ask it.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Though I certainly deserve no ill treatment from mortals, yet if the insults and repulses I receive were attended with any advantage to them, I would content myself with lamenting in silence my own unmerited indignities and man's injustice.
items.sourceLine: Though I certainly deserve no ill treatment from mortals, yet if the insults and repulses I receive were attended with any advantage to them, I would content myself with lamenting in silence my own unmerited indignities and man's injustice.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Since I would rather make of him an able man than a learned man, I would also urge that care be taken to choose a guide with a well-made rather than a well-filled head.
items.sourceLine: Since I would rather make of him an able man than a learned man, I would also urge that care be taken to choose a guide with a well-made rather than a well-filled head.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Anything done against faith or conscience is sinful.
items.sourceLine: Anything done against faith or conscience is sinful.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: For of whom any man is overcome, to the same he is also the bond-slave.
items.sourceLine: The dominion of bad men is hurtful chiefly to themselves who rule, for they destroy their own souls by greater license in wickedness; while those who are put under them in service are not hurt except by their own iniquity. items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Whatever withdraws us from the power of our senses; whatever makes the past, the distant, or the future predominate over the present, advances us in the dignity of thinking beings.
items.sourceLine: Whatever withdraws us from the power of our senses; whatever makes the past, the distant, or the future predominate over the present, advances us in the dignity of thinking beings.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: Axiom: hatred of the bourgeois is the beginning of wisdom. But I include in the word bourgeois, the bourgeois in blouses as well the bourgeois in coats. It is we and we alone, that is to say the literary men, who are the people, or to say it better: the tradition of humanity.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Avoir sa belle-mère en province quand on demeure à Paris, et vice versa, est une de ces bonnes fortunes qui se rencontrent toujours trop rarement.
items.sourceLine: Avoir sa belle-mère en province quand on demeure à Paris, et vice versa, est une de ces bonnes fortunes qui se rencontrent toujours trop rarement.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: J’enrage de bon cœur d’avoir tort, lorsque j’ai raison.
items.sourceLine: J’enrage de bon cœur d’avoir tort, lorsque j’ai raison.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, / Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
items.sourceLine: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, / Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Get your facts first, and then you can distort them as much as you please.
items.sourceLine: Get your facts first, and then you can distort them as much as you please.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: There are two classes of poets — the poets by education and practice, these we respect; and poets by nature, these we love.
items.sourceLine: There are two classes of poets — the poets by education and practice, these we respect; and poets by nature, these we love.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: Disobedience is the true foundation of liberty. The obedient must be slaves.
items.sourceLine: Disobedience is the true foundation of liberty. The obedient must be slaves.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: By the ruler's cultivation of his own character, the duties of universal obligation are set forth. By honoring men of virtue and talents, he is preserved from errors of judgment.
items.sourceLine: By the ruler's cultivation of his own character, the duties of universal obligation are set forth. By honoring men of virtue and talents, he is preserved from errors of judgment.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: Every journey begins with a single step.
items.sourceLine: Every journey begins with a single step.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: I cannot help hoping that many will feel themselves obliged to buy it. I shall not mind imagining it a disagreeable duty to them, so as they do it.
items.sourceLine: I cannot help hoping that many will feel themselves obliged to buy it. I shall not mind imagining it a disagreeable duty to them, so as they do it.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Learn What dwells in man, What is not given to man, and What men live by. When thou hast learnt these things, thou shalt return to heaven.
items.sourceLine: Go — take the mother's soul, and learn three truths: Learn What dwells in man, What is not given to man, and What men live by. When thou hast learnt these things, thou shalt return to heaven.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: A fool with a heart and no sense is just as unhappy as a fool with sense and no heart.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Once you’ve married, be strict but just with your wife, don’t allow her to forget herself, and when a misunderstanding arises, say: “Don’t forget that I made you happy.

items.quote: Sprache entsteht, wie das Bewußtsein, erst aus dem Bedürfnis, der Notdurft des Verkehrs mit anderen Menschen.

items.quote: Hypothetical liberty is allowed to everyone who is not a prisoner and in chains
items.sourceLine: Hypothetical liberty is allowed to everyone who is not a prisoner and in chains

items.quote: It is not for its own sake that men desire money, but for the sake of what they can purchase with it.
items.sourceLine: It is not for its own sake that men desire money, but for the sake of what they can purchase with it.

items.quote: The world would be astonished if it knew how great a proportion of its brightest ornaments—of those most distinguished even in popular estimation for wisdom and virtue—are complete sceptics in religion…
items.section: Ch. 2: Moral Influences in Early Youth. My Father's Character and Opinions.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Out of my own great woe I make my little songs.
items.sourceLine: Out of my own great woe I make my little songs.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Youth is always right. Those who follow the counsels of youth are wise.
items.section: Confusion of Feelings or Confusion: The Private Papers of Privy Councillor R. Von D (1927)
items.sourceLine: Youth is always right. Those who follow the counsels of youth are wise.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: It slays the weak, it slays the strong, It has a deadly stride: With iron heel it slays the strong, The monstrous parricide!
items.sourceLine: For Man's grim Justice goes its way, And will not swerve aside: It slays the weak, it slays the strong, It has a deadly stride: With iron heel it slays the strong, The monstrous parricide!

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: La raison, c'est l'intelligence en exercice; l'imagination c'est l'intelligence en érection
items.sourceLine: La raison, c'est l'intelligence en exercice; l'imagination c'est l'intelligence en érection

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: A son is a mirror in which the father sees himself reflected, and the father is a mirror in which the son sees himself as he will be in the future.
items.sourceLine: A son is a mirror in which the father sees himself reflected, and the father is a mirror in which the son sees himself as he will be in the future.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: Let the public good overcome all private and selfish regards of every kind and degree; though in truth, even private and selfish regards, and every man's own interest, will be best promoted by the preservation of peace.
items.sourceLine: Let the public good overcome all private and selfish regards of every kind and degree; though in truth, even private and selfish regards, and every man's own interest, will be best promoted by the preservation of peace.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: We were halves throughout, and to that degree that, methinks, by outliving him I defraud him of his part.
items.sourceLine: We were halves throughout, and to that degree that, methinks, by outliving him I defraud him of his part.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Reason in man is rather like God in the world.
items.sourceLine: Reason in man is rather like God in the world.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Beauty is indeed a good gift of God; but that the good may not think it a great good, God dispenses it even to the wicked.
items.sourceLine: Beauty is indeed a good gift of God; but that the good may not think it a great good, God dispenses it even to the wicked.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: There is no wisdom in useless and hopeless sorrow; but there is something in it so like virtue, that he who is wholly without it cannot be loved.
items.sourceLine: There is no wisdom in useless and hopeless sorrow; but there is something in it so like virtue, that he who is wholly without it cannot be loved.

items.author: Gustave Flaubert
items.quote: L'homme n'est rien, l'oeuvre – tout

items.quote: Entre le joueur du matin et le joueur du soir il existe la différence qui distingue le mari nonchalant de l'amant pâmé sous les fenêtres de sa belle.
items.sourceLine: Entre le joueur du matin et le joueur du soir il existe la différence qui distingue le mari nonchalant de l'amant pâmé sous les fenêtres de sa belle.

items.quote: Quare Opium facit dormire: … Quia est in eo Virtus dormitiva.
items.sourceLine: Quare Opium facit dormire: ... Quia est in eo Virtus dormitiva.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.
items.sourceLine: Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.

items.author: Mark Twain

items.sourceLine: He had only one vanity; he thought he could give advice better than any other person.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: When a whole nation is roaring Patriotism at the top of its voice, I am fain to explore the cleanness of its hands and purity of its heart.

items.quote: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live.
items.sourceLine: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Sincerity is that whereby self-completion is effected, and its way is that by which man must direct himself.
items.sourceLine: Sincerity is that whereby self-completion is effected, and its way is that by which man must direct himself.

items.author: Laozi
items.quote: Thirty spokes unite at the single hub; It is the empty space which makes the wheel useful. Mold clay to form a bowl; It is the empty space which makes the bowl useful. Cut out windows and doors; It is the empty space which makes the room useful.

items.sourceLine: I would recommend to her and Mr. D. the simple regimen of separate rooms.

items.quote: The only absolute knowledge attainable by man is that life is meaningless.
items.sourceLine: The only absolute knowledge attainable by man is that life is meaningless.

items.quote: A widow, the mother of a family, and from her heart she produces chords to which my whole being responds.
items.sourceLine: A widow, the mother of a family, and from her heart she produces chords to which my whole being responds.

items.quote: Ours is a lost generation, it may be, but it is more blameless than those earlier generations.

items.quote: We speak not strictly and philosophically when we talk of the combat of passion and of reason. Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.

items.quote: I frequently asked myself, if I could, or if I was bound to go on living, when life must be passed in this manner. I generally answered to myself, that I did not think I could possibly bear it beyond a year.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
items.sourceLine: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: We believe that out of the public school grows the greatness of a nation.
items.sourceLine: We believe that out of the public school grows the greatness of a nation.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: There is a freemasonry among the dull by which they recognize and are sociable with the dull, as surely as a correspondent tact in men of genius.
items.sourceLine: There is a freemasonry among the dull by which they recognize and are sociable with the dull, as surely as a correspondent tact in men of genius.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: Some circumstantial evidence is very strong, as when you find a trout in the milk.
items.sourceLine: Some circumstantial evidence is very strong, as when you find a trout in the milk.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: The way of Heaven and Earth may be completely declared in one sentence: They are without any doubleness, and so they produce things in a manner that is unfathomable.
items.sourceLine: The way of Heaven and Earth may be completely declared in one sentence: They are without any doubleness, and so they produce things in a manner that is unfathomable.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves, it is not my nature.
items.sourceLine: There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves, it is not my nature.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: Ivan Ilych's life had been most simple and most ordinary and therefore most terrible.
items.sourceLine: Ivan Ilych's life had been most simple and most ordinary and therefore most terrible.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: It's easier for a Russian to become an atheist than for anyone else in the world.
items.sourceLine: It's easier for a Russian to become an atheist than for anyone else in the world.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: A fiancé is neither this nor that: he’s left one shore, but not yet reached the other.
items.sourceLine: A fiancé is neither this nor that: he’s left one shore, but not yet reached the other.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The object of art — like every other product — creates a public which is sensitive to art and enjoys beauty.
items.sourceLine: The object of art — like every other product — creates a public which is sensitive to art and enjoys beauty.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: The Messiah will come only when he is no longer necessary; he will come only on the day after his arrival; he will come, not on the last day, but on the very last day.
items.sourceLine: The Messiah will come only when he is no longer necessary; he will come only on the day after his arrival; he will come, not on the last day, but on the very last day.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind. The understanding can intuit nothing, the senses can think nothing. Only through their unison can knowledge arise.
items.sourceLine: Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind. The understanding can intuit nothing, the senses can think nothing. Only through their unison can knowledge arise.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Man sollte alle Tage wenigstens ein kleines Lied hören, ein gutes Gedicht lesen, ein treffliches Gemälde sehen und, wenn es möglich zu machen wäre, einige vernünftige Worte sprechen.
items.sourceLine: Man sollte alle Tage wenigstens ein kleines Lied hören, ein gutes Gedicht lesen, ein treffliches Gemälde sehen und, wenn es möglich zu machen wäre, einige vernünftige Worte sprechen.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: My task is to throw a light on that which we must always love and revere, of which no subsequent knowledge can rob us: man in his greatness.
items.section: Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks (posthumous)
items.sourceLine: My task is to throw a light on that which we must always love and revere, of which no subsequent knowledge can rob us: man in his greatness.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: For the purpose of acquiring gain, everything else is pushed aside or thrown overboard, for example, as is philosophy by the professors of philosophy.
items.section: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life
items.sourceLine: For the purpose of acquiring gain, everything else is pushed aside or thrown overboard, for example, as is philosophy by the professors of philosophy.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: After the devil himself, there is no worse folk than the pope and his followers.
items.sourceLine: And I myself, in Rome, heard it said openly in the streets, “If there is a hell, then Rome is built on it.” That is, “After the devil himself, there is no worse folk than the pope and his followers.”

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: The first thing that we know about ourselves is our imperfection. This is what Descartes meant when he said: 'I know God before I know myself.' The only mark of God in us is that we feel that we are not God.
items.sourceLine: The first thing that we know about ourselves is our imperfection. This is what Descartes meant when he said: 'I know God before I know myself.' The only mark of God in us is that we feel that we are not God.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: It is not possible to run a course aright when the goal itself has not been rightly placed.
items.sourceLine: It is not possible to run a course aright when the goal itself has not been rightly placed.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: By 'idea' I understand a conception of the mind which the mind forms by reason of its being a thinking thing.
items.sourceLine: From Descartes and Malebranche onward, the metaphysical value of the “idea” or archetype steadily deteriorated. It became a “thought,” an internal condition of cognition, as clearly formulated by Spinoza: “By 'idea' I understand a conception of the mind which the mind forms by reason of its being a thinking thing.” Finally Kant reduced the archetypes to a limited number of categories of understanding.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: In our reasonings concerning matter of fact, there are all imaginable degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty to the lowest species of moral evidence. A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
items.sourceLine: In our reasonings concerning matter of fact, there are all imaginable degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty to the lowest species of moral evidence. A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: To expect, indeed, that the freedom of trade should ever be entirely restored in Great Britain, is as absurd as to expect that an Oceana or Utopia should never be established in it.
items.sourceLine: To expect, indeed, that the freedom of trade should ever be entirely restored in Great Britain, is as absurd as to expect that an Oceana or Utopia should never be established in it.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.
items.sourceLine: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: One should forgive one's enemies, but not before they are hanged.
items.sourceLine: One should forgive one's enemies, but not before they are hanged.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: He looked at her again, now with the vague abject shyness that older men often have with young women, as though asking their indulgence for no longer being young.
items.section: The Post Office Girl (published posthumously in 1982)
items.sourceLine: He looked at her again, now with the vague abject shyness that older men often have with young women, as though asking their indulgence for no longer being young.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: All charming people, I fancy, are spoiled. It is the secret of their attraction.
items.sourceLine: All charming people, I fancy, are spoiled. It is the secret of their attraction.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: One can no more pray too much than love too much.
items.sourceLine: One can no more pray too much than love too much.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: I have needed God every day to defend myself against the abundance of thoughts.
items.section: The Point of View of My Work as an Author (1848)
items.sourceLine: I have needed God every day to defend myself against the abundance of thoughts.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: A constant element of enjoyment must be mingled with our studies, so that we think of learning as a game rather than a form of drudgery, for no activity can be continued for long if it does not to some extent afford pleasure to the participant.
items.sourceLine: A constant element of enjoyment must be mingled with our studies, so that we think of learning as a game rather than a form of drudgery, for no activity can be continued for long if it does not to some extent afford pleasure to the participant.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: He who does not give himself leisure to be thirsty cannot take pleasure in drinking.
items.sourceLine: He who does not give himself leisure to be thirsty cannot take pleasure in drinking.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: We can open our hearts to God, but only with Divine help.
items.sourceLine: We can open our hearts to God, but only with Divine help.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Quantum in te crescit amor, tantum crescit pulchritudo; quia ipsa caritas est animae pulchritudo.
items.section: Ten Homilies on the First Epistle of John (414)
items.sourceLine: Quantum in te crescit amor, tantum crescit pulchritudo; quia ipsa caritas est animae pulchritudo.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Here closed in death th' attentive eyes That saw the manners in the face.
items.sourceLine: Here closed in death th' attentive eyes That saw the manners in the face.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Les musiciennes sont presque toujours amoureuses. Celle qui chantait ainsi devait savoir bien aimer.
items.section: Part II: A Woman Without a Heart
items.sourceLine: Les musiciennes sont presque toujours amoureuses. Celle qui chantait ainsi devait savoir bien aimer.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: On voit qu'il se travaille à dire de bons mots.
items.sourceLine: On voit qu'il se travaille à dire de bons mots.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: We are such stuff As dreams are made on; and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
items.sourceLine: We are such stuff As dreams are made on; and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Now what I contend is that my body is my own, at least I have always so regarded it. If I do harm through my experimenting with it, it is I who suffer, not the state.
items.sourceLine: Now what I contend is that my body is my own, at least I have always so regarded it. If I do harm through my experimenting with it, it is I who suffer, not the state.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: A sect or party is an elegant incognito devised to save a man from the vexation of thinking.
items.sourceLine: A sect or party is an elegant incognito devised to save a man from the vexation of thinking.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: You must love the crust of the earth on which you dwell more than the sweet crust of any bread or cake; you must be able to extract nutriment out of a sand heap.
items.sourceLine: You must love the crust of the earth on which you dwell more than the sweet crust of any bread or cake; you must be able to extract nutriment out of a sand heap.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: They are without any doubleness, and so they produce things in a manner that is unfathomable.
items.sourceLine: The way of Heaven and Earth may be completely declared in one sentence: They are without any doubleness, and so they produce things in a manner that is unfathomable.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: It was in this reign that Joan of Arc reigned and made such a row among the English.
items.sourceLine: It was in this reign that Joan of Arc reigned and made such a row among the English.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: If one has no vanity in this life of ours, there is no sufficient reason for living.
items.sourceLine: If one has no vanity in this life of ours, there is no sufficient reason for living.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness to yourself. Watch over your own deceitfulness and look into it every hour, every minute.
items.sourceLine: Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness to yourself. Watch over your own deceitfulness and look into it every hour, every minute.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Only during hard times do people come to understand how difficult it is to be master of their feelings and thoughts.
items.sourceLine: Only during hard times do people come to understand how difficult it is to be master of their feelings and thoughts.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The individual produces an object and, by consuming it, returns to himself, but returns as a productive and self reproducing individual. Consumption thus appears as a moment of production.
items.sourceLine: The individual produces an object and, by consuming it, returns to himself, but returns as a productive and self reproducing individual. Consumption thus appears as a moment of production.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Das Böse weiß vom Guten, aber das Gute vom Bösen nicht. Selbsterkenntnis hat nur das Böse. - Die Acht Oktavhefte; published by BookRix, 9-8-2014.
items.sourceLine: Das Böse weiß vom Guten, aber das Gute vom Bösen nicht. Selbsterkenntnis hat nur das Böse. - Die Acht Oktavhefte; published by BookRix, 9-8-2014.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Psychologists have hitherto failed to realize that imagination is a necessary ingredient of perception itself.
items.sourceLine: Psychologists have hitherto failed to realize that imagination is a necessary ingredient of perception itself.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: To know of someone here and there whom we accord with, who is living on with us, even in silence — this makes our earthly ball a peopled garden.
items.sourceLine: To know of someone here and there whom we accord with, who is living on with us, even in silence — this makes our earthly ball a peopled garden.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: The only thing of interest in a refuted system is the personal element. It alone is what is forever irrefutable.
items.section: Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks (posthumous)
items.sourceLine: The only thing of interest in a refuted system is the personal element. It alone is what is forever irrefutable.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: The fundament upon which all our knowledge and learning rests is the inexplicable.
items.sourceLine: The fundament upon which all our knowledge and learning rests is the inexplicable.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: Tell your master that if there were as many devils at Worms as tiles on its roofs, I would enter.
items.sourceLine: Tell your master that if there were as many devils at Worms as tiles on its roofs, I would enter.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: It is frequently stated that Descartes was the first to apply algebra to geometry. This statement is inaccurate, for Vieta and others had done this before him. Even the Arabs sometimes used algebra in connection with geometry.
items.sourceLine: It is frequently stated that Descartes was the first to apply algebra to geometry. This statement is inaccurate, for Vieta and others had done this before him. Even the Arabs sometimes used algebra in connection with geometry.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: But by far the greatest obstacle to the progress of science and to the undertaking of new tasks and provinces therein is found in this — that men despair and think things impossible.
items.sourceLine: But by far the greatest obstacle to the progress of science and to the undertaking of new tasks and provinces therein is found in this — that men despair and think things impossible.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: If I should name myself after anyone, then I know no one other better.
items.sourceLine: If I should name myself after anyone, then I know no one other better.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: Where men are the most sure and arrogant, they are commonly the most mistaken, and have there given reins to passion, without that proper deliberation and suspense, which can alone secure them from the grossest absurdities.
items.section: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals (1751)
items.sourceLine: Where men are the most sure and arrogant, they are commonly the most mistaken, and have there given reins to passion, without that proper deliberation and suspense, which can alone secure them from the grossest absurdities.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: In public, as well as in private expences, great wealth may, perhaps, frequently be admitted as an apology for great folly.
items.sourceLine: In public, as well as in private expences, great wealth may, perhaps, frequently be admitted as an apology for great folly.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: ..Whenever it ceases to be true that mankind, as a rule, prefer themselves to others, and those nearest to them to those more remote, from that moment Communism is not only practicable, but the only defensible form of society…
items.sourceLine: ..Whenever it ceases to be true that mankind, as a rule, prefer themselves to others, and those nearest to them to those more remote, from that moment Communism is not only practicable, but the only defensible form of society...

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Experience is a good school. But the fees are high.
items.sourceLine: Experience is a good school. But the fees are high.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Confidences are always risky: a secret entrusted to a stranger make him less of one. You've given away something of yourself, given him the advantage.
items.section: The Post Office Girl (published posthumously in 1982)
items.sourceLine: Confidences are always risky: a secret entrusted to a stranger make him less of one. You've given away something of yourself, given him the advantage.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: It is always a silly thing to give advice, but to give good advice is absolutely fatal.
items.sourceLine: It is always a silly thing to give advice, but to give good advice is absolutely fatal.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: The best way to worship God is to love your wife.
items.sourceLine: The best way to worship God is to love your wife.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: He lived year after year. He attended only to himself and to God and this picture-but he did not understand himself.
items.sourceLine: He lived year after year. He attended only to himself and to God and this picture-but he did not understand himself.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: In regione caecorum rex est luscus.
items.sourceLine: In regione caecorum rex est luscus.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.
items.sourceLine: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: Truth is the ultimate end of the whole universe.
items.sourceLine: Truth is the ultimate end of the whole universe.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: The inclination to seek the truth is safer than the presumption which regards unknown things as known.
items.sourceLine: The inclination to seek the truth is safer than the presumption which regards unknown things as known.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Books that you may carry to the fire, and hold readily in your hand, are the most useful after all.
items.sourceLine: Books that you may carry to the fire, and hold readily in your hand, are the most useful after all.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Les gens sans esprit ressemblent aux mauvaises herbes qui se plaisent dans les bons terrains, et ils aiment d'autant plus être amusés qu'ils s'ennuient eux-mêmes.
items.sourceLine: Les gens sans esprit ressemblent aux mauvaises herbes qui se plaisent dans les bons terrains, et ils aiment d'autant plus être amusés qu'ils s'ennuient eux-mêmes.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Les doutes sont fâcheux plus que toute autre chose.
items.sourceLine: Les doutes sont fâcheux plus que toute autre chose.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: This Booke When Brasse and Marble fade, shall make thee looke Fresh to all Ages.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: This Booke When Brasse and Marble fade, shall make thee looke Fresh to all Ages.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Always do right. This will gratify some people, and astonish the rest.
items.sourceLine: Always do right. This will gratify some people, and astonish the rest.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: No man can have society upon his own terms. If he seeks it, he must serve it too.
items.sourceLine: No man can have society upon his own terms. If he seeks it, he must serve it too.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: He who gives himself entirely to his fellow-men appears to them useless and selfish; but he who gives himself partially to them is pronounced a benefactor and philanthropist.
items.sourceLine: He who gives himself entirely to his fellow-men appears to them useless and selfish; but he who gives himself partially to them is pronounced a benefactor and philanthropist.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Only by perfect virtue can the perfect path, in all its courses, be made a fact.
items.sourceLine: How great is the path proper to the Sage! Like overflowing water, it sends forth and nourishes all things, and rises up to the height of heaven. All-complete is its greatness! It embraces the three hundred rules of ceremony, and the three thousand rules of demeanor. It waits for the proper man, and then it is trodden. Hence it is said, "Only by perfect virtue can the perfect path, in all its courses, be made a fact."

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: There were several Battles between the Yorkists and the Lancastrians, in which the former (as they ought) usually won.
items.sourceLine: There were several Battles between the Yorkists and the Lancastrians, in which the former (as they ought) usually won.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: To be good and lead a good life means to give to others more than one takes from them.
items.sourceLine: To be good and lead a good life means to give to others more than one takes from them.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive but in finding something to live for.
items.sourceLine: For the mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive but in finding something to live for.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: The thirst for powerful sensations takes the upper hand both over fear and over compassion for the grief of others.
items.sourceLine: The thirst for powerful sensations takes the upper hand both over fear and over compassion for the grief of others.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: But there is a devil of a difference between barbarians who are fit by nature to be used for anything, and civilized people who apply them selves to everything.
items.sourceLine: But there is a devil of a difference between barbarians who are fit by nature to be used for anything, and civilized people who apply them selves to everything.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: …it is not necessary to accept everything as true, one must only accept it as necessary.' 'A melancholy conclusion,' said K. 'It turns lying into a universal principle.In the Cathedral
items.sourceLine: '...it is not necessary to accept everything as true, one must only accept it as necessary.' 'A melancholy conclusion,' said K. 'It turns lying into a universal principle.In the Cathedral

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: I have no knowledge of myself as I am, but merely as I appear to myself.
items.sourceLine: I have no knowledge of myself as I am, but merely as I appear to myself.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Die Kunst ist lang, das Leben kurz, das Urteil schwierig, die Gelegenheit flüchtig.
items.sourceLine: Die Kunst ist lang, das Leben kurz, das Urteil schwierig, die Gelegenheit flüchtig.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: The concept of greatness is changeable, in the realm of morality as well as in that of esthetics. And so philosophy starts by legislating greatness.
items.section: Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks (posthumous)
items.sourceLine: The concept of greatness is changeable, in the realm of morality as well as in that of esthetics. And so philosophy starts by legislating greatness.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: All the cruelty and torment of which the world is full is in fact merely the necessary result of the totality of the forms under which the will to live is objectified.
items.sourceLine: All the cruelty and torment of which the world is full is in fact merely the necessary result of the totality of the forms under which the will to live is objectified.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: A penny saved is of more value than a penny paid out (Der Sparpfennig ist reicher denn der Zinspfenning).
items.sourceLine: A penny saved is of more value than a penny paid out (Der Sparpfennig ist reicher denn der Zinspfenning).

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Mais apud me omnia fiunt Mathematicè in Natura
items.sourceLine: Mais apud me omnia fiunt Mathematicè in Natura

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: My Lord St. Albans said that Nature did never put her precious jewels into a garret four stories high, and therefore that exceeding tall men had ever very empty heads.
items.sourceLine: My Lord St. Albans said that Nature did never put her precious jewels into a garret four stories high, and therefore that exceeding tall men had ever very empty heads.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Had the barber but known what sort of a creature Spinoza was, he certainly would not have spoken of his blessed memory.
items.sourceLine: Spinoza died on the 21st of February, 1677, in the forty-fourth year of his age. The cause of his death was consumption, from which he had long been a sufferer; this was in harmony with his system of philosophy, according to which all particularity and individuality pass away in the one substance. items.author: David Hume
items.quote: From the comparison of theism and idolatry, we may form some other observations, which will also confirm the vulgar observation that the corruption of the best things gives rise to the worst.
items.sourceLine: From the comparison of theism and idolatry, we may form some other observations, which will also confirm the vulgar observation that the corruption of the best things gives rise to the worst.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The government of an exclusive company of merchants is, perhaps, the worst of all governments for any country whatever.
items.sourceLine: The government of an exclusive company of merchants is, perhaps, the worst of all governments for any country whatever.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: In my education, as in that of everyone, the moral influences, which are so much more important than all others, are also the most complicated, and the most difficult to specify with any approach to completeness.
items.section: Ch. 2: Moral Influences in Early Youth. My Father's Character and Opinions.
items.sourceLine: In my education, as in that of everyone, the moral influences, which are so much more important than all others, are also the most complicated, and the most difficult to specify with any approach to completeness.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Whatever tears one may shed, in the end one always blows one's nose.
items.sourceLine: Whatever tears one may shed, in the end one always blows one's nose.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Hairdressers are professional gossips; when only the hands are busy, the tongue is seldom still.
items.section: The Post Office Girl (published posthumously in 1982)
items.sourceLine: Hairdressers are professional gossips; when only the hands are busy, the tongue is seldom still.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Art finds her own perfection within, and not outside of herself. She is not to be judged by any external standard of resemblance. She is a veil, rather than a mirror.
items.sourceLine: Art finds her own perfection within, and not outside of herself. She is not to be judged by any external standard of resemblance. She is a veil, rather than a mirror.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: Je représente un parti qui n'existe pas encore, le parti Révolution-Civilisation. Ce parti fera le vingtième siècle. Il en sortira d'abord les États-Unis d'Europe, puis les États-Unis du Monde.
items.sourceLine: Je représente un parti qui n'existe pas encore, le parti Révolution-Civilisation. Ce parti fera le vingtième siècle. Il en sortira d'abord les États-Unis d'Europe, puis les États-Unis du Monde.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: I can understand myself in believing, although in addition I can in a relative misunderstanding comprehend the human aspect of this life: but comprehend faith or comprehend Christ, I cannot.
items.sourceLine: I can understand myself in believing, although in addition I can in a relative misunderstanding comprehend the human aspect of this life: but comprehend faith or comprehend Christ, I cannot.

items.author: Erasmus
items.quote: I doubt if a single individual could be found from the whole of mankind free from some form of insanity. The only difference is one of degree. A man who sees a gourd and takes it for his wife is called insane because this happens to very few people.
items.sourceLine: I doubt if a single individual could be found from the whole of mankind free from some form of insanity. The only difference is one of degree. A man who sees a gourd and takes it for his wife is called insane because this happens to very few people.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Quand je me joue à ma chatte, qui sait si elle passe son temps de moi, plus que je ne fais d'elle.
items.sourceLine: Quand je me joue à ma chatte, qui sait si elle passe son temps de moi, plus que je ne fais d'elle.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: I, what I love, and the love itself. … There are, therefore three things: the lover, the beloved and the love.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Fly fishing may be a very pleasant amusement; but angling or float fishing I can only compare to a stick and a string, with a worm at one end and a fool at the other.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Entre personnes sans cesse en présence, la haine et l'amour vont toujours croissant: on trouve à tout moment des raisons pour s'aimer ou se haïr mieux.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Others abide our question. Thou art free. We ask and ask—Thou smilest and art still, Out-topping knowledge.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: He is a stranger to me, but he is a most remarkable man — and I am the other one. Between us, we cover all knowledge; he knows all that can be known, and I know the rest.

items.sourceLine: Probably nature itself gave man the ability to lie so that in difficult and tense moments he could protect his nest, just as do the vixen and wild duck.

items.quote: Money does not arise by convention, any more than the state does. It arises out of exchange, and arises naturally out of exchange; it is a product of the same.

items.quote: It is therefore correct to say that the senses do not err — not because they always judge rightly, but because they do not judge at all.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Doesn't surprise me that Christ our Lord preferred to live with whores & sinners, seeing I go in for that myself.

items.quote: Mathematics would certainly have not come into existence if one had known from the beginning that there was in nature no exactly straight line, no actual circle, no absolute magnitude.

items.quote: If you feel irritated by the absurd remarks of two people whose conversation you happen to overhear, you should imagine that you are listening to a dialogue of two fools in a comedy.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: I think that I think, therefore I think that I am;
items.sourceLine: CARTESIAN, adj. Relating to Descartes, a famous philosopher, author of the celebrated dictum, Cogito ergo sum -- whereby he was pleased to suppose he demonstrated the reality of human existence. The dictum might be improved, however, thus: Cogito cogito ergo cogito sum -- "I think that I think, therefore I think that I am;" as close an approach to certainty as any philosopher has yet made.

items.quote: Like strawberry wives, that laid two or three great strawberries at the mouth of their pot, and all the rest were little ones.

items.quote: There are more fools in the world than there are people.
items.sourceLine: There are more fools in the world than there are people.

items.quote: There is nothing more vindictive, nothing more underhanded, than a little world that would like to be a big one.

items.quote: Like the body the soul can be healthy, youthful, and so on. It can undergo pain, thirst, and hunger. In this physical life, that is, in the visible world, we avoid whatever would defile or deform the body; how much more, then, ought we to avoid that which would tarnish the soul?

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: His character does not appear more extraordinary and unusual by the mixture of so much absurdity with so much penetration, than by his tempering such violent ambition, and such enraged fanaticism with so much regard to justice and humanity.
items.sourceLine: His character does not appear more extraordinary and unusual by the mixture of so much absurdity with so much penetration, than by his tempering such violent ambition, and such enraged fanaticism with so much regard to justice and humanity.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Upstart greatness is everywhere less respected than ancient greatness.
items.sourceLine: Upstart greatness is everywhere less respected than ancient greatness.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Whenever the general disposition of the people is such, that each individual regards those only of his interests which are selfish, and does not dwell on, or concern himself for, his share of the general interest, in such a state of things, good government is impossible.
items.sourceLine: Whenever the general disposition of the people is such, that each individual regards those only of his interests which are selfish, and does not dwell on, or concern himself for, his share of the general interest, in such a state of things, good government is impossible.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: When I am with my sweetheart kind, A happy youth am I; So great the wealth within my mind, I the whole world could buy. But when her swanlike arms I quit, In that sad hour of pain, Away my boasted wealth doth flit, And I am poor again.
items.sourceLine: When I am with my sweetheart kind, A happy youth am I; So great the wealth within my mind, I the whole world could buy. But when her swanlike arms I quit, In that sad hour of pain, Away my boasted wealth doth flit, And I am poor again.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Something indefinite is always worse than something definite, a strong fear that doesn't last very long is easier than one that's nebulous but doesn't go away.
items.section: The Post Office Girl (published posthumously in 1982)
items.sourceLine: Something indefinite is always worse than something definite, a strong fear that doesn't last very long is easier than one that's nebulous but doesn't go away.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: He to whom the present is the only thing that is present, knows nothing of the age in which he lives.
items.sourceLine: He to whom the present is the only thing that is present, knows nothing of the age in which he lives.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: I will be Chateaubriand or nothing.
items.sourceLine: I will be Chateaubriand or nothing.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: If the genius is an artist, then he accomplishes his work as art, but neither he nor his work of art has a telos outside him.
items.sourceLine: If the genius is an artist, then he accomplishes his work as art, but neither he nor his work of art has a telos outside him.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: To an atheist all writings tend to atheism: he corrupts the most innocent matter with his own venom.
items.sourceLine: To an atheist all writings tend to atheism: he corrupts the most innocent matter with his own venom.

items.author: Thomas Aquinas
items.quote: If man of himself could in a perfect manner know all things visible and invisible, it would indeed be foolish to believe what he does not see. But our manner of knowing is so weak that no philosopher could perfectly investigate the nature of even one little fly.
items.sourceLine: If man of himself could in a perfect manner know all things visible and invisible, it would indeed be foolish to believe what he does not see. But our manner of knowing is so weak that no philosopher could perfectly investigate the nature of even one little fly.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Bad times, hard times, this is what people keep saying; but let us live well, and times shall be good. We are the times: Such as we are, such are the times.
items.sourceLine: Bad times, hard times, this is what people keep saying; but let us live well, and times shall be good. We are the times: Such as we are, such are the times.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: Ignorance in other men may be censured as idleness, in an academick it must be abhorred as treachery.
items.sourceLine: Ignorance in other men may be censured as idleness, in an academick it must be abhorred as treachery.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Notre cœur est un trésor, videz-le d'un coup, vous êtes ruinés. Nous ne pardonnons pas plus à un sentiment de s'être montré tout entier qu'à un homme de ne pas avoir un sou à lui.
items.sourceLine: Notre cœur est un trésor, videz-le d'un coup, vous êtes ruinés. Nous ne pardonnons pas plus à un sentiment de s'être montré tout entier qu'à un homme de ne pas avoir un sou à lui.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Le véritable Amphitryon, Est l'Amphitryon où l'on dine.
items.sourceLine: Le véritable Amphitryon, Est l'Amphitryon où l'on dine.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Mellifluous Shakespeare, whose enchanting Quill Commandeth Mirth or Passion, was but Will.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: Mellifluous Shakespeare, whose enchanting Quill Commandeth Mirth or Passion, was but Will.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: Thunder is good, thunder is impressive; but it is lightning that does the work.
items.sourceLine: Thunder is good, thunder is impressive; but it is lightning that does the work.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: The best effect of fine persons is felt after we have left their presence.
items.sourceLine: The best effect of fine persons is felt after we have left their presence.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: The vessel, though her masts be firm, Beneath her copper bears a worm.
items.sourceLine: The vessel, though her masts be firm, Beneath her copper bears a worm.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Among the appliances to transform the people, sound and appearances are but trivial influences.
items.sourceLine: Among the appliances to transform the people, sound and appearances are but trivial influences.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: One does not love a place the less for having suffered in it, unless it has been all suffering, nothing but suffering.
items.sourceLine: One does not love a place the less for having suffered in it, unless it has been all suffering, nothing but suffering.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: I know nothing about the governmental organization, or in how far it is good or bad, and for the same reason I do not want to support it.
items.section: The Kingdom of God is Within You (1894)
items.sourceLine: The revolutionaries say: "The government organization is bad in this and that respect; it must be destroyed and replaced by this and that." But a Christian says: "I know nothing about the governmental organization, or in how far it is good or bad, and for the same reason I do not want to support it."

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: In most cases, people, even the most vicious, are much more naive and simple-minded than we assume them to be. And this is true of ourselves too.
items.sourceLine: In most cases, people, even the most vicious, are much more naive and simple-minded than we assume them to be. And this is true of ourselves too.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: Country acquaintances are charming only in the country and only in the summer. In the city in winter they lose half of their appeal.
items.sourceLine: Country acquaintances are charming only in the country and only in the summer. In the city in winter they lose half of their appeal.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: In fact of course, this 'productive' worker cares as much about the crappy shit he has to make as does the capitalist himself who employs him, and who also couldn't give a damn for the junk.
items.sourceLine: In fact of course, this 'productive' worker cares as much about the crappy shit he has to make as does the capitalist himself who employs him, and who also couldn't give a damn for the junk.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Hey, there’s something falling down in there," said the chief clerk. Gregor tried to suppose to himself that what had happened to him might some day also happen to the chief clerk. There was no denying that anything was possible.
items.sourceLine: "Hey, there’s something falling down in there," said the chief clerk. Gregor tried to suppose to himself that what had happened to him might some day also happen to the chief clerk. There was no denying that anything was possible.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: Philosophical knowledge is the knowledge gained by reason from concepts; mathematical knowledge is the knowledge gained by reason from the construction of concepts.
items.sourceLine: Philosophical knowledge is the knowledge gained by reason from concepts; mathematical knowledge is the knowledge gained by reason from the construction of concepts.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: The fate of the architect is the strangest of all. How often he expends his whole soul, his whole heart and passion, to produce buildings into which he himself may never enter.
items.sourceLine: The fate of the architect is the strangest of all. How often he expends his whole soul, his whole heart and passion, to produce buildings into which he himself may never enter.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: The degree of introspection achieved by Nietzsche had never been achieved by anyone, nor is it ever likely to be achieved again.
items.sourceLine: The degree of introspection achieved by Nietzsche had never been achieved by anyone, nor is it ever likely to be achieved again.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Buying books would be a good thing if one could also buy the time to read them in: but as a rule the purchase of books is mistaken for the appropriation of their contents.
items.sourceLine: Buying books would be a good thing if one could also buy the time to read them in: but as a rule the purchase of books is mistaken for the appropriation of their contents.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: Since the law is good, the will, which is hostile to it, cannot be good.
items.sourceLine: Since the law is good, the will, which is hostile to it, cannot be good.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: You're overlooking a key feature of the phenomenon,
items.sourceLine: "Do you know who first explained the true origin of the rainbow?" I asked. "It was Descartes," he said. After a moment he looked me in the eye. "And what do you think was the salient feature of the rainbow that inspired Descartes' mathematical analysis?" he asked. "Well, the rainbow is actually a section of a cone that appears as an arc of the colors of the spectrum when drops of water are illuminated by sunlight beh

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Alonso of Aragon was wont to say in commendation of age, that age appears to be best in four things — old wood best to burn, old wine to drink, old friends to trust, and old authors to read.
items.sourceLine: Alonso of Aragon was wont to say in commendation of age, that age appears to be best in four things — old wood best to burn, old wine to drink, old friends to trust, and old authors to read.

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Nothing is less Greek than the conceptual web-spinning of a hermit—amor intellectualis dei—after the fashion of Spinoza.
items.sourceLine: Nothing is less Greek than the conceptual web-spinning of a hermit—amor intellectualis dei—after the fashion of Spinoza.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: But though all the general rules of art are founded only on experience and on the observation of the common sentiments of human nature, we must not imagine, that, on every occasion, the feelings of men will be conformable to these rules.
items.sourceLine: But though all the general rules of art are founded only on experience and on the observation of the common sentiments of human nature, we must not imagine, that, on every occasion, the feelings of men will be conformable to these rules.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The tolls for the maintenance of a high road, cannot with any safety be made the property of private persons.
items.sourceLine: The tolls for the maintenance of a high road, cannot with any safety be made the property of private persons.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Whatever we may think or affect to think of the present age, we cannot get out of it; we must suffer with its sufferings, and enjoy with its enjoyments; we must share in its lot, and, to be either useful or at ease, we must even partake its character.
items.sourceLine: Whatever we may think or affect to think of the present age, we cannot get out of it; we must suffer with its sufferings, and enjoy with its enjoyments; we must share in its lot, and, to be either useful or at ease, we must even partake its character.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Every woman is the gift of a world to me.
items.sourceLine: Every woman is the gift of a world to me.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: No one would ever believe how hard it is to be really alone in a city of millions when you don't have money.
items.section: The Post Office Girl (published posthumously in 1982)
items.sourceLine: No one would ever believe how hard it is to be really alone in a city of millions when you don't have money.

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Psycholog­y is in its infancy, as a science. I hope in the interests of Art, it will always remain so.
items.sourceLine: Psycholog­y is in its infancy, as a science. I hope in the interests of Art, it will always remain so.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: L'œil était dans la tombe et regardait Caïn.
items.sourceLine: L'œil était dans la tombe et regardait Caïn.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Here you see what it is to be a human being; but he adds: Take care, for I am also God — blessed is he who takes no offense at me.
items.sourceLine: Out of love, God becomes man. He says: Here you see what it is to be a human being; but he adds: Take care, for I am also God — blessed is he who takes no offense at me.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: L'homme est bien insensé. Il ne saurait forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines.
items.sourceLine: L'homme est bien insensé. Il ne saurait forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: He who created us without our help will not save us without our consent.
items.sourceLine: He who created us without our help will not save us without our consent.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: A desire for knowledge is the natural feeling of mankind; and every human being, whose mind is not debauched, will be willing to give all he has to get knowledge.
items.sourceLine: A desire for knowledge is the natural feeling of mankind; and every human being, whose mind is not debauched, will be willing to give all he has to get knowledge.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: L'homme est imparfait. Il est parfois plus ou moins hypocrite, et les niais disent alors qu'il a ou n'a pas de mœurs.
items.sourceLine: L'homme est imparfait. Il est parfois plus ou moins hypocrite, et les niais disent alors qu'il a ou n'a pas de mœurs.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Vous parlez devant un homme à qui tout Naples est connu.
items.sourceLine: Vous parlez devant un homme à qui tout Naples est connu.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: The stream of Time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabrics of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakspere.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: The stream of Time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabrics of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakspere.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: The easy confidence with which I know another man's religion is folly teaches me to suspect that my own is also.
items.sourceLine: The easy confidence with which I know another man's religion is folly teaches me to suspect that my own is also.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: How we hate this solemn Ego that accompanies the learned, like a double, wherever he goes.
items.sourceLine: How we hate this solemn Ego that accompanies the learned, like a double, wherever he goes.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: Most books belong to the house and streets only, and in the fields their leaves feel very thin.
items.sourceLine: Most books belong to the house and streets only, and in the fields their leaves feel very thin.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: Things have their root and their branches. Affairs have their end and their beginning. To know what is first and what is last will lead near to what is taught in the Great Learning.
items.sourceLine: Things have their root and their branches. Affairs have their end and their beginning. To know what is first and what is last will lead near to what is taught in the Great Learning.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: A lady, without a family, was the very best preserver of furniture in the world.
items.sourceLine: A lady, without a family, was the very best preserver of furniture in the world.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: The government organization is bad in this and that respect; it must be destroyed and replaced by this and that.
items.section: The Kingdom of God is Within You (1894)
items.sourceLine: The revolutionaries say: "The government organization is bad in this and that respect; it must be destroyed and replaced by this and that." But a Christian says: "I know nothing about the governmental organization, or in how far it is good or bad, and for the same reason I do not want to support it."

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: Men reject their prophets and slay them, but they love their martyrs and honor those they have slain.
items.sourceLine: Men reject their prophets and slay them, but they love their martyrs and honor those they have slain.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: If you can’t distinguish people from lap-dogs, you shouldn’t undertake philanthropic work.
items.sourceLine: If you can’t distinguish people from lap-dogs, you shouldn’t undertake philanthropic work.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: Although usury is itself a form of credit in its bourgeoisified form, the form adapted to capital, in its pre-bourgeois form it is rather the expression of the lack of credit.
items.sourceLine: Although usury is itself a form of credit in its bourgeoisified form, the form adapted to capital, in its pre-bourgeois form it is rather the expression of the lack of credit.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: The whole visible world is perhaps nothing more than the rationalization of a man who wants to find peace for a moment. An attempt to falsify the actuality of knowledge, to regard knowledge as a goal still to be reached.
items.sourceLine: The whole visible world is perhaps nothing more than the rationalization of a man who wants to find peace for a moment. An attempt to falsify the actuality of knowledge, to regard knowledge as a goal still to be reached.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: For it is extremely absurd to expect to be enlightened by reason, and yet to prescribe to her beforehand on which side she must incline.
items.sourceLine: For it is extremely absurd to expect to be enlightened by reason, and yet to prescribe to her beforehand on which side she must incline.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: Let us live in as small a circle as we will, we are either debtors or creditors before we have had time to look round.
items.sourceLine: Let us live in as small a circle as we will, we are either debtors or creditors before we have had time to look round.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: The philosopher John Searle once told me that reading Nietzsche was like drinking cognac — a sip was good, but you didn't want to drink the whole bottle.
items.sourceLine: The philosopher John Searle once told me that reading Nietzsche was like drinking cognac — a sip was good, but you didn't want to drink the whole bottle.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: Jede Trennung gibt einen Vorgeschmack des Todes und jedes Wiedersehen einen Vorgeschmack der Auferstehung.
items.sourceLine: Jede Trennung gibt einen Vorgeschmack des Todes und jedes Wiedersehen einen Vorgeschmack der Auferstehung.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, "Repent," he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.
items.sourceLine: When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, "Repent," he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: So blind is the curiosity by which mortals are possessed, that they often conduct their minds along unexplored routes, having no reason to hope for success, but merely being willing to risk the experiment of finding whether the truth they seek lies there.
items.sourceLine: So blind is the curiosity by which mortals are possessed, that they often conduct their minds along unexplored routes, having no reason to hope for success, but merely being willing to risk the experiment of finding whether the truth they seek lies there.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: Cosmus, Duke of Florence, was wont to say of perfidious friends, that "We read that we ought to forgive our enemies; but we do not read that we ought to forgive our friends.
items.sourceLine: Cosmus, Duke of Florence, was wont to say of perfidious friends, that "We read that we ought to forgive our enemies; but we do not read that we ought to forgive our friends."

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: He who loves God,” Spinoza says, “cannot strive that God should love him in return.
