items.author: David Hume
items.quote: The same good sense, that directs men in the ordinary occurrences of life, is not hearkened to in religious matters, which are supposed to be placed altogether above the cognizance of human reason.
items.sourceLine: The same good sense, that directs men in the ordinary occurrences of life, is not hearkened to in religious matters, which are supposed to be placed altogether above the cognizance of human reason.

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: The education of the common people requires, perhaps, in a civilized and commercial society, the attention of the public more than that of people of some rank and fortune.
items.sourceLine: The education of the common people requires, perhaps, in a civilized and commercial society, the attention of the public more than that of people of some rank and fortune.

items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.quote: Il regardait toute secte comme nuisible,
items.section: Ch. 4: Youthful Propagandism. The Westminster Review.
items.sourceLine: [T]he correct statement would be, not that I disliked poetry, but that I was theoretically indifferent to it. I disliked any sentiments in poetry which I should have disliked in prose; and that included a great deal. And I was wholly blind to its place in human culture, as a means of educating the feelings. But I was always personally very susceptible to some kinds of it. ...Long before I had enlarged in any consider

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: When words leave off, music begins.
items.sourceLine: When words leave off, music begins.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: It always demands a far greater degree of courage for an individual to oppose an organized movement than to let himself be carried along with the stream
items.sourceLine: It always demands a far greater degree of courage for an individual to oppose an organized movement than to let himself be carried along with the stream — individual courage, that is, a variety of courage that is dying out in these times of progressive organization and mechanization. During the war practically the only courage I ran across was mass courage, the courage that comes of being one of a herd, and anyone wh

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: Prayer must never be answered: if it is, it ceases to be prayer and becomes correspondence.
items.sourceLine: Prayer must never be answered: if it is, it ceases to be prayer and becomes correspondence.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: There shall be no slavery of the mind.
items.sourceLine: There shall be no slavery of the mind.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: Out of love, God becomes man. He says: Here you see what it is to be a human being; but he adds: Take care, for I am also God — blessed is he who takes no offense at me.
items.sourceLine: Out of love, God becomes man. He says: Here you see what it is to be a human being; but he adds: Take care, for I am also God — blessed is he who takes no offense at me.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Ceux qui ont apparié notre vie à un songe ont eu de la raison. … Nous veillons dormants et veillants dormons.
items.sourceLine: Ceux qui ont apparié notre vie à un songe ont eu de la raison. ... Nous veillons dormants et veillants dormons.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: So the Church too, like Mary, enjoys perpetual virginity and uncorrupted fecundity.
items.sourceLine: So the Church too, like Mary, enjoys perpetual virginity and uncorrupted fecundity.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: It is more from carelessness about truth than from intentional lying, that there is so much falsehood in the world.
items.sourceLine: It is more from carelessness about truth than from intentional lying, that there is so much falsehood in the world.

items.author: Honoré de Balzac
items.quote: Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu'il a été proprement fait.
items.sourceLine: Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu'il a été proprement fait.

items.author: Molière
items.quote: Ah, la belle chose que de savoir quelque chose.
items.sourceLine: Ah, la belle chose que de savoir quelque chose.

items.author: William Shakespeare
items.quote: Scorn not the Sonnet. Critic, you have frowned, Mindless of its just honours; with this key Shakespeare unlocked his heart.
items.section: Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations
items.sourceLine: Scorn not the Sonnet. Critic, you have frowned, Mindless of its just honours; with this key Shakespeare unlocked his heart.

items.author: Mark Twain
items.quote: You tell me whar a man gits his corn pone, en I'll tell you what his 'pinions is.
items.sourceLine: You tell me whar a man gits his corn pone, en I'll tell you what his 'pinions is.

items.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.quote: People do not deserve to have good writing, they are so pleased with bad.
items.sourceLine: People do not deserve to have good writing, they are so pleased with bad.

items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.quote: The finest workers in stone are not copper or steel tools, but the gentle touches of air and water working at their leisure with a liberal allowance of time.
items.sourceLine: The finest workers in stone are not copper or steel tools, but the gentle touches of air and water working at their leisure with a liberal allowance of time.

items.author: Confucius
items.quote: When the Great Dao (Tao, perfect order) prevails, the world is like a Commonwealth State shared by all, not a dictatorship.
items.section: A Great Utopia (The World of Da-Tong)
items.sourceLine: When the Great Dao (Tao, perfect order) prevails, the world is like a Commonwealth State shared by all, not a dictatorship.

items.author: Jane Austen
items.quote: It was, perhaps, one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides.
items.sourceLine: It was, perhaps, one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides.

items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.quote: The only significance of life consists in helping to establish the kingdom of God; and this can be done only by means of the acknowledgment and profession of the truth by each one of us.
items.section: The Kingdom of God is Within You (1894)
items.sourceLine: The only significance of life consists in helping to establish the kingdom of God; and this can be done only by means of the acknowledgment and profession of the truth by each one of us.

items.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
items.quote: So long as man remains free he strives for nothing so incessantly and so painfully as to find some one to worship.
items.sourceLine: So long as man remains free he strives for nothing so incessantly and so painfully as to find some one to worship.

items.author: Anton Chekhov
items.quote: It is not only the prisoners who grow coarse and hardened from corporeal punishment, but those as well who perpetrate the act or are present to witness it.
items.sourceLine: It is not only the prisoners who grow coarse and hardened from corporeal punishment, but those as well who perpetrate the act or are present to witness it.

items.author: Karl Marx
items.quote: The circulation of capital realizes value, while living labour creates value.
items.sourceLine: The circulation of capital realizes value, while living labour creates value.

items.author: Franz Kafka
items.quote: Idleness is the beginning of all vice, the crown of all virtues.
items.sourceLine: Idleness is the beginning of all vice, the crown of all virtues.

items.author: Immanuel Kant
items.quote: The inscrutable wisdom through which we exist is not less worthy of veneration in respect to what it denies us than in respect to what it has granted.
items.sourceLine: The inscrutable wisdom through which we exist is not less worthy of veneration in respect to what it denies us than in respect to what it has granted.

items.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
items.quote: No one would talk much in society, if he knew how often he misunderstands others.
items.sourceLine: No one would talk much in society, if he knew how often he misunderstands others.

items.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
items.quote: Strauss’ whole study indicates that noble nature as Nietzsche presents it—no, embodies it—replaces divine nature as Plato presents it.
items.sourceLine: Strauss’ whole study indicates that noble nature as Nietzsche presents it—no, embodies it—replaces divine nature as Plato presents it.

items.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
items.quote: We can come to look upon the deaths of our enemies with as much regret as we feel for those of our friends, namely, when we miss their existence as witnesses to our success.
items.sourceLine: We can come to look upon the deaths of our enemies with as much regret as we feel for those of our friends, namely, when we miss their existence as witnesses to our success.

items.author: Martin Luther
items.quote: To say that the cross emblazoned with the papal coat of arms, and set up by the indulgence preachers, is equal in worth to the cross of Christ is blasphemy.
items.sourceLine: To say that the cross emblazoned with the papal coat of arms, and set up by the indulgence preachers, is equal in worth to the cross of Christ is blasphemy.

items.author: René Descartes
items.quote: Newton's proof of the law of refraction is based on an erroneous notion that light travels faster in glass than in air, the same error that Descartes had made. This error stems from the fact that both of them thought that light was corpuscular in nature.
items.sourceLine: Newton's proof of the law of refraction is based on an erroneous notion that light travels faster in glass than in air, the same error that Descartes had made. This error stems from the fact that both of them thought that light was corpuscular in nature.

items.author: Francis Bacon
items.quote: We read that we ought to forgive our enemies; but we do not read that we ought to forgive our friends.
items.sourceLine: Cosmus, Duke of Florence, was wont to say of perfidious friends, that "We read that we ought to forgive our enemies; but we do not read that we ought to forgive our friends."

items.author: Baruch Spinoza
items.quote: Of all the philosophers of the seventeenth century, perhaps none have more relevance today than Spinoza.
items.sourceLine: Of all the philosophers of the seventeenth century, perhaps none have more relevance today than Spinoza.

items.author: David Hume
items.quote: I say, then, that belief is nothing but a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object, than what the imagination alone is ever able to attain
items.sourceLine: I say, then, that belief is nothing but a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object, than what the imagination alone is ever able to attain

items.author: Adam Smith
items.quote: Fear is in almost all cases a wretched instrument of government, and ought in particular never to be employed against any order of men who have the smallest pretensions to independency.
items.sourceLine: Fear is in almost all cases a wretched instrument of government, and ought in particular never to be employed against any order of men who have the smallest pretensions to independency.

items.author: Heinrich Heine
items.quote: Oaks shall be rent; the Word shall shatter
items.sourceLine: Oaks shall be rent; the Word shall shatter — Yea, on that fiery day, the Crown, Even the palace walls shall totter, And domes and spires come crashing down.

items.author: Stefan Zweig
items.quote: Why is it that the stupidest people are always the most good-natured?
items.sourceLine: Why is it that the stupidest people are always the most good-natured?

items.author: Oscar Wilde
items.quote: An idea that is not dangerous is unworthy of being called an idea at all.
items.sourceLine: An idea that is not dangerous is unworthy of being called an idea at all.

items.author: Victor Hugo
items.quote: To divinise is human, to humanise is divine.
items.sourceLine: To divinise is human, to humanise is divine.

items.author: Søren Kierkegaard
items.quote: The truth is a trap: you can not get it without it getting you; you cannot get the truth by capturing it, only by its capturing you.
items.sourceLine: The truth is a trap: you can not get it without it getting you; you cannot get the truth by capturing it, only by its capturing you.

items.author: Michel de Montaigne
items.quote: Physicians have this advantage: the sun lights their success and the earth covers their failures.
items.sourceLine: Physicians have this advantage: the sun lights their success and the earth covers their failures.

items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.quote: Nobody should ever doubt that in the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5) absolutely all sins, from the least to the greatest, are altogether forgiven.
items.sourceLine: Nobody should ever doubt that in the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5) absolutely all sins, from the least to the greatest, are altogether forgiven.

items.author: Samuel Johnson
items.quote: There can be no friendship without confidence, and no confidence without integrity.
items.sourceLine: There can be no friendship without confidence, and no confidence without integrity.
